articles.title_orig: Djokovic claims 7th China Open men's singles title, Andreeva powers into last 8
articles.title_zh: Djokovic claims 7th China Open men's singles title, Andreeva powers into last 8
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING - Serbian veteran Novak Djokovic claimed his seventh China Open men's singles title, while Russia's Mirra Andreeva reached the women's singles quarterfinals with a straight-set victory here on Tuesday.
Djokovic, 39, who previously won the China Open in 2009, 2010 and from 2012 to 2015, continued his perfect record at the tournament. The 24-time Grand Slam champion came from behind to defeat top seed Alexander Zverev of Germany in the quarterfinals before advancing to the final after third seed Daniil Medvedev of Russia was defaulted while trailing in the semifinals.
Facing 27-year-old Alex de Minaur in the final, Djokovic won the first set 7-6 (3). The Australian led 1-0 in the second before retiring with a left adductor strain. The victory extended Djokovic's China Open winning streak to 34 matches, with the Serbian having won the title in all seven of his appearances at the tournament.
"The great is not something that you are born with. It's something that really needs to be built. Individual sport like tennis requires 100 percent of commitments and dedication to this sport, not only when it comes to training, but when it comes to full lifestyle," Djokovic noted.
Asked whether this would be his last appearance at the China Open, the Serbian said, "We will see. I will be back for sure, but in which role and how... I don't know yet to be honest. I am not making plans for so far ahead right now."
In the men's doubles final, British pair Julian Cash and Lloyd Glasspool took the title after defeating the Netherlands' Sander Arends and David Pel 6-3, 3-6, 10-6.
ALSO READ: China Open: Djokovic meets De Minaur in final, Zheng into round 16
On the women's side, fourth seed Andreeva eased past Ukraine's Daria Snigur 6-2, 6-2. "I think today I was serving and defending well because she (Snigur) is a very aggressive player. I thought being a good defender today would be good and useful," said Andreeva.
"I feel more comfortable with every match that I get to play. I think that's a good sign. I try my best to keep up the same level of intensity because I really want to advance further and win more matches," the 19-year-old Russian added. She will next meet compatriot Ekaterina Alexandrova.
The Czech Republic's Karolina Muchova and Nikola Bartunkova also reached the quarterfinals after defeating Japan's Naomi Osaka and Austria's Sinja Kraus respectively on Tuesday, setting up an all-Czech clash.
Just four days after contesting the women's singles final at the Asian Games in Nagoya, China's Wang Xiyu and Zhang Shuai returned to action in the women's doubles first round at the China Open.
Asian Games champion Wang and compatriot Jiang Xinyu lost to Chinese Taipei's Hsieh Su-wei and Latvia's Jelena Ostapenko 6-1, 1-6, 10-4. Asian Games silver medalist Zhang, 37, partnered the Czech Republic's Katerina Siniakova to beat China's Yuan Yue and Feng Shuo 6-1, 7-6 (4).
"Coming back from Nagoya to here, it was only a two-day turnaround. Everything in my life revolves around tennis. I eat, sleep, and take a break. Everything is for better tennis. This is what a professional tennis player should do," veteran Zhang said.
READ MORE: China Open: Zheng advances as Shang earns Zverev showdown
On Wednesday, third seed Coco Gauff of the United States will face Belgium's Elise Mertens, while China's Zheng Qinwen will take on Armenia's Alina Charaeva.

articles.title_orig: From million-dollar mansions to surveillance missions, the life and travels of an alleged Chinese agent
articles.title_zh: From million-dollar mansions to surveillance missions, the life and travels of an alleged Chinese agent
articles.content_orig:
Three years before California realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang was arrested as an alleged Chinese agent , she showed up in San Francisco celebrating the visit of President Xi Jinping.
Zhang was photographed in 2023 wearing a red cap and marching on the street alongside the leader of a Chinese American organization with deep ties to the Beijing government's foreign influence arm.
Soon after the photo was taken, pro-Chinese Communist Party activists there began assaulting protesters of Xi's authoritarian regime — though there is no evidence Zhang was involved in any attacks.
The Orange County mother, 34, is now facing federal prosecution for allegedly surveilling the Taiwanese president's son in Washington last year at the direction of Chinese government officials.
The FBI said it has obtained her text messages with Chinese intelligence officials, plotting and executing a plan to secretly film Taiwan's first son, Lai Ting-yu, and his family in the Seattle suburb where they live.
Investigators even allege they have footage from a neighbor's security camera catching Zhang in the midst of her surveillance mission.
A CBS News investigation reveals the alleged agent's backstory bears striking similarities with infamous suspected Chinese spy Fang "Christine" Fang, who had an intimate relationship with disgraced congressman Eric Swalwell before fleeing to China in 2015 amid an FBI espionage probe.
Like Fang, Zhang attended the University of International Relations in Beijing, which is run by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's intelligence agency and secret police.
In a criminal complaint filed in a Los Angeles court, FBI counterintelligence special agent Kevin Holt wrote that the ministry "recruits heavily" from the university.
After moving to the U.S., Zhang studied at the University of Southern California and got her real estate license in 2016.
She built her business as a realtor with Irvine-based JC Pacific Corp over the next decade, listing over 130 properties, according to Zillow, with prices ranging from the hundreds of thousands to upwards of $8 million.
Zhang and her husband, a fellow realtor at JC Pacific, bought their six-bedroom, 6,030-square-foot home for $5.65 million in 2024, records show. They sold the property in June for $6 million.
Her Instagram page shows curated photos of Zhang in designer clothing, dining at expensive restaurants, taking trips around the U.S. and Canada, and shopping at luxury stores with a friend in Paris last year.
Similar to Fang, she became involved in advocacy groups and events for Chinese Americans.
In 2022 she attended an "entrepreneurship competition" for Chinese students with Chinese government consulate officials, and was honored at an event for "Chinese young elites in the United States" the same year where she was given a " young entrepreneur " award.
Her involvement in the All American Chinese Association brought her in contact with officials who had deep ties to the Chinese government.
AACA's leader, Cai Chenghua, was vice chair of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, a U.S. group so close to the Beijing government it had to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act as an influence arm of the Chinese Communist Party.
In 2022 Cai helped organize a celebration of China's National Day at which the Los Angeles consul general Zhang Ping urged Chinese Americans to oppose "Taiwan independence" and support China's "complete reunification."
AACA bused in pro-China supporters to San Francisco for President Xi's visit in November 2023. Zhang was photographed alongside Cai, wearing matching red caps behind an AACA banner.
AACA board member Tian Jun is also a committee member in the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office, which became part of the Chinese government's United Front in 2018, according to research by Michael Lucci , a security consultant who helps protect U.S. institutions from Chinese influence through his firm, State Armor.
Cai has been photographed at several events with former Arcadia, California, Mayor Eileen Wang, who pleaded guilty to acting as a Chinese government agent in May.
"U.S.-based groups linked to the Communist Party's United Front through their key personnel keep coming up in federal foreign-agent cases," Jacqueline Deal, an adviser to State Armor, told CBS News."This is not a coincidence. The mission of these organizations is to help the Party and hurt the United States."
At a minimum, Deal said officers from these groups should have to register with the U.S. Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. That's the federal law Zhang is alleged to have violated by acting as a Chinese agent without registering as required.
Cai has not been accused of any wrongdoing or charged with any crime. He did not respond to a request for comment.
According to prosecutors, by 2025 Zhang had fully embraced a role as a Chinese government agent.
She traveled to China in January that year and met a government official and fellow graduate of the University of International Relations, the FBI affidavit said.
Two months later, the pair texted on Chinese messaging app WeChat about the address of a Taiwanese official who spoke out against the Chinese government, according to records obtained by a search warrant of Zhang's iCloud account, the FBI agent wrote.
She allegedly visited China again in June and met with a second Chinese official in the private room of a restaurant, where investigators believe she received her mission to surveil the Taiwanese president's son.
She later texted her alleged government handler: "I can take care of this thing."
After recording video of Lai and his family, she returned to LA without incident, according to the complaint. She was arrested while attempting to board a flight to Shanghai at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday.
She appeared in court on Monday dressed in the same designer workout gear she was wearing during the arrest.
Her family declined to comment.
"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, in a statement released Monday.
"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals," he said.
A spokesperson for the Taiwanese president told CBS News he condemns "such brutal acts of suppression, intimidation, and even harm to the freedom and democracy of people or their families, which are unacceptable in the civilized world."
"We thank the US judicial agency for their assistance and protection to our people," the spokesperson said. "Taiwan will continue to cooperate with all democratic allies to jointly combat illegal acts of cross-border repression."
The Chinese Foreign Ministry did not respond to CBS News' request for comment. A spokesperson  told NBC News,  "China has always opposed hyped-up accusations of 'China spying' that slander and smear the country."

articles.title_zh: China’s DeepZang AI aims to transform Tibetan language tech, promote unity
articles.content_orig:
Seminar attended by the LLM’s developer discusses expanding multi-dialect translation, public service integration and cross-regional AI
Approaches to advancing the large language model, DeepZang, were discussed at a seminar on Monday that brought together representatives from research institutes, universities and enterprises, according to state-run portal Chinanews.com.
It said the event held in Hohhot, in China’s northern Inner Mongolia autonomous region, addressed issues such as improving Tibetan artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and expanding the model’s application into multilingual simultaneous interpretation.
Speakers included Tenzin Norbu, the model’s founder, who vowed to continuously refine Tibetan AI technologies and advance their practical use. He also emphasised the use of technological innovation to “foster ethnic interaction and integration” and support digital development in ethnic minority regions.

articles.title_orig: Trump will not reimburse federal government for taxpayer-funded advertisements
articles.title_zh: Trump will not reimburse federal government for taxpayer-funded advertisements
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump hedged Tuesday when asked whether he would reimburse the U.S. government for previously aired television advertisements that praised him, saying, "We'll decide."
The ads cost the federal government nearly $10 million before Trump on Monday announced that he and his political action committee will pay for the segments in the face of criticism that they are propaganda and aimed at helping Republican political candidates.
The White House later Monday clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service announcements going forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. The prior airings reportedly were funded from a pool of up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security .
Asked whether he would reimburse the government for the costs of ads already aired, Trump told reporters, "The ads were really good."
"They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before," he said. "So we'll decide."
Trump's latest comments on the furor came hours after a new ad aired. That ad was labeled as paid for by the U.S. government.
The ad features video clips of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussing the U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.
"Nicolás Maduro had his chance ... until he didn't," Hegseth says in the ad. "He effed around and he found out."
Another clip in the ad shows Rubio warning, "Don't play games with [President Trump] in office."
The ads have been running in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election . Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress.
The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately reply when asked whether the super PAC would cover the cost of the new ad or whether the buy had already been placed before Trump's announcement and would remain taxpayer-funded.
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday.
"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said.
AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5.
Trump's announcement that he would pay for the ads came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter,  reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency."
The Times said federal money to pay for the ads became available on Sept. 19, "when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department.
Sen. Maggie Hassan , D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'"
In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with."
"They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," Hassan said.
"There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account," she said.
On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called for the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate the ads.
"The government is not the President's campaign committee, and the Treasury is not his campaign account. The federal government has no legitimate business billing the public for campaign messaging that a candidate's political committee should pay for," Schumer wrote in a letter .
Last week, the advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint urging the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Trade Commission and TV broadcasters to stop airing the ads. Public Citizen previously asked the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate whether the ads violated federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act. That law restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns.
MAGA Inc. has raised $424.4 million and spent $32.4 million during the 2025-26 cycle through Aug. 31, leaving the Trump Super PAC with $415.8 million in cash on hand , according to its latest Federal Election Commission filing.
MAGA Inc. has spent at least $57 million this election cycle, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings, including $25 million in independent expenditures reported since the end of August.

articles.title_orig: Tropical threat brewing in Gulf could impact U.S. as a hurricane this weekend. See maps, possible path.
articles.title_zh: Tropical threat brewing in Gulf could impact U.S. as a hurricane this weekend. See maps, possible path.
articles.content_orig:
With less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season , the potential for a ninth named tropical storm in the Atlantic basin is brewing in the southern Gulf.
Since the Atlantic's season began on June 1, it has only seen eight named storms this year, while El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The season ends Nov. 30.
Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Gulf on Tuesday. As the storm brews over the warmer waters off Mexico, it's expected to become a tropical storm by early Wednesday and a hurricane on Thursday, according to the National Hurricane Center.
If it does become a tropical storm, it would receive the name Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs."
Forecast models are beginning to come to agreement that the northward motion of this tropical system brings it to the Gulf Coast this weekend.
Regardless of its name or if it develops into a tropical storm, we do know that it will bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week.
Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.
Timing, storm intensity and severity of impacts to land with this tropical system are what remain unknown.
While some models have impacts starting Friday evening, others show it beginning later in the weekend.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."
While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.
The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).
When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

articles.title_orig: Soybeans left out of U.S.-China trade talks; Minnesota farmer weighs in
articles.title_zh: Soybeans left out of U.S.-China trade talks; Minnesota farmer weighs in
articles.content_orig:
ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – Soybeans were excluded from the U.S.-China trade talks in late September. The lack of discussion on the crop was not what the American Soybean Association (ASA) hoped for.
“ASA is disappointed U.S. soybeans were not included among the agricultural products receiving additional tariff relief from China,” the organization wrote on its website. “China’s remaining 10% retaliatory duty limits access for private Chinese importers, meaning soybean trade will continue to be handled primarily by China’s state-owned enterprises. Removing the tariff would improve the competitiveness of U.S. soybeans and provide greater opportunity for private Chinese buyers.”
According to ASA, China is committed to 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans annually for 2026, 2027 and 2028.
“Any time we talk about trade in China, it’s always big news,” said Darin Johnson, who is the director of the Minnesota Soybean Growers Association. “We were a little bit let down about the lack of discussion about soybeans and trade going into the future.”
Johnson is a fourth-generation Faribault County soybean farmer. He said he was generally happy that the trade talks happened; however, it would have been ideal if the existing tariff on the agricultural product had been cut.
“The 10% tariff remains on, which is unfortunate for us as a US soybean producer,” Johnson said. “It puts us at a competitive disadvantage globally, unfortunately, especially against our biggest competitor: South America.”
KTTC spoke with University of Minnesota McKnight Professor of Applied Economics Carlisle Runge regarding the topic. He said the lack of discussion is damaging for Midwestern soybean producers.
“The Chinese want to maintain the soybean trade as leverage for further negotiations,” Runge said. “By most estimates, the trade in soybeans with China has fallen year on year anywhere from 50% to 75%.”
As a farmer, Johnson said input costs have been the main concern. He said crop prices have been better.
“We’re pretty lucky to be able to have an opportunity to be able to at least start selling some of our commodities, at least above break even at this point,” Johnson said. “Things are starting to look a little bit brighter.”
Minnesota is the third-largest state exporter of soybeans to China. Iowa and Illinois rank first and second.

articles.title_orig: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after surviving a failed execution attempt last week, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, her attorneys said in a statement on Tuesday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995, survived two failed lethal injections last Wednesday in Tennessee. She was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical.
Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented. She is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection.
Her lawyers called her progress "medically unprecedented", and while her prognosis remains unclear, "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There were seven other cases where prisoners survived slated executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected," she said.
"They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," Denno said. "This has never happened before."
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong after injecting her with the chemical pentobarbital.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he plans to resign.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Pike's attorneys are scheduled to appear in court in Nashville on Wednesday. They also plan to hold a news conference outside the court.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said on Tuesday that the likelihood of recovering from lethal injection is low.
"Most people who get lethal injection die from it," he told the BBC. "In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa. So, the fact that she survived it ... was unusual."
But there remains a lot of uncertainty and many unknowns, he said, including how much of the pentobarbital got into her system, what her blood levels were after the injection and what her recovery will look like.
"I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he noted.
Zivot had previously said the two doses of pentobarbital she received last week would have been enough that, had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation, "she would have surely died".
Instead, Zivot said a possible explanation is that instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.
Zivot said last week he thought her ending up with a brain injury was "very possible", due to the delays in resuscitating her. He also believed it would take about a week to truly understand her condition and do a neurological exam. It's now been six days since the failed attempt to execute her.
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
They said on Tuesday that she has endured "severe damage" to her arms.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks information about such cases.
For lethal injections, such incidents have typically occurred due to difficulty obtaining reliable IV access to the veins, though the underlying reason differs from person to person.
In cases the centre has documented, all failures happened before the lethal  drugs could be administered. The last failed lethal injection that was tracked happened earlier this year - also in Tennessee.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.

articles.title_orig: California couple with 21 children, most born via surrogates, charged in ‘house of horrors’ abuse case
articles.title_zh: California couple with 21 children, most born via surrogates, charged in ‘house of horrors’ abuse case
articles.content_orig:
A Southern California couple who had 21 children , most of whom were birthed by different surrogate mothers, lied to the surrogates and then subjected the children to vicious beatings and punishments, authorities said.
Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan were arrested Tuesday after authorities served a search warrant at their Arcadia mansion as part of a child abuse investigation. They have been charged with conspiracy to commit child abuse and witness intimidation.
Xuan also faces one felony count of child abuse, one felony count of accessory after the fact and five felony counts of dissuading a witness. Zhang also faces one count of accessory after the fact and four counts of dissuading a witness.
In court Tuesday afternoon, they pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations.
“This house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredibly young children,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said at a Tuesday news conference.
Authorities began investigating the couple last year after a 2-month-old child was brought to the hospital with head injuries. Hochman, citing a criminal complaint, alleged that a nanny struck the baby in the head on May 4, 2025.
Xuan and Zhang did not seek medical attention until days later, he said, noting that the baby has since recovered.
During the investigation, authorities learned that Xuan and Zhang were running a surrogacy ring out of their home and hired surrogates throughout the country.
Hochman said the couple often lied to the women about why they wanted children or how many children they already had .
“One surrogate in particular … was paid for both a first and second surrogacy,” he said. “She was told initially Zhang was a single mother struggling to conceive when she agreed to act as a surrogate. That was a false statement.”
The woman was paid up to $75,000 per surrogacy, the district attorney said.
The couple failed to tell another woman who was seven months pregnant that they already had 16 children, he said.
“Another surrogate, they said they were seeking the miracle baby, and they paid that surrogate $135,000,” Hochman said.
Over the years, the children were allegedly abused while Xuan and Zhang watched on 32 motion-activated cameras they set up around the home, Hochman said.
He described three rooms the couple called “learning rooms,” where the children would spend hours seated at desks under the supervision of various nannies.
“Each one of these defendants monitored the nannies’ discipline of the children that were happening in the three learning centers,” the district attorney said.
He said during one incident, a nanny had forced a child “to maintain a horse stance” and Xuan could be seen on video laughing.
“In another situation, defendant Xuan entered one of the learning centers while a nanny was striking a child, and instructed the nanny to strike the child harder,” he said.
Hochman alleged that Xuan also beat a child across the child’s bare buttocks and struck the child’s head.
“Defendant Xuan also lifted the child into the air by one arm, while continuing to strike him and repeatedly struck the child’s head from side to side with sufficient force that the child’s body lurched into alternating directions with the blows,” he told reporters.
He said the children were punished, physically abused and beaten “on a daily basis.”
One room in the home did not have cameras. Hochman said the children would be taken into the room and could be heard “screaming from inside.”
The couple is accused of trying to cover up the alleged abuse by instructing the children to lie, according to Hochman. During a meeting after the 2-month-old was taken to the hospital, the couple allegedly told the nannies not to leave visible marks on the children.
“This case is unprecedented,” Hochman said. “It is horrific, and the physical abuse, beating, and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.”
Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert G. Luna said the children were subjected to “horrific abuse.”
All 21 children are now in state custody.
Prosecutors sought $100 million bail per person because of the serious nature of the charges and because authorities said the pair are flight risks.
The judge set bail at $20 million each with home detention and a protective order against visiting their children.
A bail review hearing has been set for Monday.
An arrest warrant was previously issued for one of the nannies seen on video violently shaking the 2-month-old baby. The nanny has not been arrested.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 rose to an all-time intraday on Tuesday, touching 7844.52 and surpassing its August 13 intraday peak when it hit 7,830. The benchmark also closed for the first time over 7,800.
The recovery comes after months of oil shocks, rising borrowing costs and the possible start of a Federal Reserve rate hiking cycle.
The record rally comes just a day after the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5.3%, reaching levels not seen since 2002. In mid September, the Fed raised its benchmark rate for the first time in over three years and indicated more were to come.
Oil had crossed $100 a barrel in early March for the first time since 2022 as the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz. After falling below $70 a barrel, it slingshot back above $100 in early September.
"At the end of the day, oil and bond yields can be correlated, but so is the stock market and profits. And if the profits are there, which they have been, the stock market is going to be resilient, even if the economy is a bit more mixed," Shawn Snyder, economic strategist at Potomac Fund Management, told CNBC.
Unlike prior records this year, this latest run has been narrowly lead by a few stocks tied to the AI hype and deemed unfettered by adverse macroeconomic headwinds.
"When traders take a breather from the noise surrounding them — much of it negative in recent months — and look closer at what's happening in the markets, it becomes clear the U.S. stock market is the best place to park their money compared with other locations. It's hard to argue against the mostly positive risk-reward ratio we've seen over multiple decades," said JJ Kinahan, Cboe Global Markets senior vice president of retail and alternative investments.
The so-called Magnificent 7 namely, Nvidia , Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft and Tesla make up more than 34% of the market cap of the S&P 500 .
"When you consider that much girth among a small handful of stocks, it's apparent how much these stocks' daily movements dictate the direction of the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, both of which are in record territory again today," Kinahan said.
With tech companies investing heavily in data centers and computing infrastructure demand for chips and equipment has gone up. Earlier this year, Amazon said it expected about $200 billion in capital expenditures across its businesses in 2026, citing opportunities including AI, chips and robotics.
Investor appetite for ambitious technology bets also became evident in June, when SpaceX raised $75 billion in the largest IPO ever and began trading on June 12. The debut became another milestone where investors continued backing growth companies despite higher energy prices and borrowing costs.
Looking ahead, however, Potomac Fund Management's Snyder cautioned that the "weakening" market breadth may last longer if inflation shows no signs of easing, or if there's no clear signal that the Federal Reserve is achieving its mandate. The central bank is slated to release its minutes from the September meeting on Wednesday.
The market "can look relatively calm, but there are still things going on underneath the surface that may not be so calm," Snyder said.

Drone attack sinks ship off NATO ally Bulgaria as expert warns Russia is ‘taking things up a notch’.
A commercial ship sank and its crew vanished Tuesday after an apparent coordinated air-and-sea drone attack off NATO member Bulgaria, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia before warning Moscow was preparing a broader "massive strike."
A second vessel was also heavily damaged and set ablaze inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, with a drone expert warning the dual precision strikes signaled a dangerous escalation and possible "larger invasion posture" by Russia.
"They were likely using the Geran-4 aerial drone to take the vessel out or the Maran surface vehicle to take it out," Cameron Chell, founder of drone manufacturer Draganfly , told Fox News Digital on Tuesday of the first strike.

"The reason it wasn't just an air vehicle or an air drone that took this ship out was that the Gerans generally come in at a pretty steep angle when they're on final attack," Chell said.
"There are not really any precision drones that fly closely above the surface, which is where they would have had to hit in order to create an impact that would sink this ship fast enough," he added.
"The nature of this strike suggests there was a combination of an air attack and surface attack," Chell said.
The dual attack occurred roughly 70 nautical miles off the eastern Bulgarian coastal town of Byala, according to Reuters , bringing the conflict into the economic zone of a NATO member.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence and security services were working to determine the full circumstances surrounding the attack.

"Our Navy contacted its counterparts in Bulgaria, and it has been established that this was a combined Russian attack using maritime and aerial drones."
Chell suggested the attack’s location and hybrid nature could serve Russia by sowing greater uncertainty across the region.
"We can see the amount of geopolitical chaos that's involved, and this is exactly the type of thing that would benefit Russia in the region," Chell said.
"The hybrid element here is really blurring the lines between traditional military actions," he added, describing the attack as "an expansion of strategy and tactics."
"This is indicative of this larger invasion posture that seems to be unfolding for Russia," Chell said. "And a real desire, what appears to be, for Russia to take things up a notch."

A nearby Bulgarian ferry, the Dioscuria, diverted to the scene after witnessing an explosion and receiving distress signals, Reuters reported.
Rescuers found an overturned lifeboat, life rafts and life jackets floating in the debris field.

"Not only are you using pretty sophisticated equipment, but you're also doing it in a coordinated manner," Chell said.

"These things coordinated and were struck relatively at the same time. So another level of coordination has unfolded here," Chell added.

"Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," Radev told reporters.

Chell said striking the two ships inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone could also have the effect of disrupting a crucial shipping corridor and creating fear among commercial operators.
"It all adds up to a perfect little scenario for the Russians to create chaos there, not just to disrupt the lane of economics for the region and in particular for Ukraine — a lifeline," Chell said.
"The Russians are really taking a playbook out of the Iranians who have basically created enough chaos in the Strait of Hormuz where the operators can't take the chance to put their ships through there," he added.
The strikes came amid a surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident off Romania’s coast Monday in which two people died in a ship fire.

articles.title_orig: France shuts down nearly 900 schools as violent education protests escalate
articles.title_zh: France shuts down nearly 900 schools as violent education protests escalate
articles.content_orig:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 6,000 people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.
Authorities estimate hundreds of thousands of protesters, including students, teachers and delegates from trade unions, took to the streets on Tuesday as protests sweep the country.
In Paris, tear gas filled the air, and trash cans, school desks and chairs were set alight as riot police with shields and batons clashed with some demonstrators.
The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.
“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”
Despite their suburban beginnings, the protests are now drawing international attention. US President Donald Trump claimed Tuesday that “what’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.”
“This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.
The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.
A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.
Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).
There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”
The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.
France’s interior ministry estimated there were about 256,000 protesters out on the streets nationwide on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris. Meanwhile, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, one of the high school student unions involved in organizing the demonstrations, suggested a much larger turnout of 450,000 people across the country.
More than 400 people were detained in Tuesday’s protests, the ministry said.
Some students have called for fresh demonstrations on Thursday.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, said “extreme violence has reached the gates of our high schools and it must be condemned unequivocally.”
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 education staff have been injured during the unrest, calling it “the highest number of education staff injured in decades.” He rejected accusations that the government had ordered police to repress the protests.
He also said officials must listen to the concerns and demands of students at each school.
“That is why time will be set aside starting this week, from Wednesday, to allow each leadership team to organize a session of internal democracy within its high school,” he wrote on X.
The Education Ministry has launched an online portal where students can share their concerns and ideas for improving their education.
The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.
The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.
Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”
The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.
CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne, Lucie Lepellec, Kate Irby and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Sheen effect, innovative storytelling and 'renewed energy' mark World Mission Sunday at 100
articles.title_zh: Sheen effect, innovative storytelling and 'renewed energy' mark World Mission Sunday at 100
articles.content_orig:
(OSV News) ─ Catholics around the world will mark World Mission Sunday on Oct. 18, and a "renewed energy" infuses the annual celebration of the Church's missionary activity this milestone year, one expert told OSV News.
"There are more and more dioceses around the country that are finding innovative ways to tell the stories of missionaries, and the need to support missionaries, the need to pray for missionaries," said Father Anthony D. Andreassi, a priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri in Brooklyn, New York, and a researcher for the Pontifical Mission Societies USA.
Pope Leo XIV has chosen the theme "One in Christ, united in mission" for this year's celebration, with his message for the day encouraging "the whole Church to continue its missionary journey with joy and zeal in the Holy Spirit."
Established by Pope Pius XI in 1926 and universally observed by 1927, World Mission Sunday is a dedicated day of "prayer and missionary promotion throughout the Catholic world," according to its founding decree.
Masses celebrated on the observance, which takes place on the next-to-last Sunday in October, are offered for the Church's missions, with priests encouraged to preach homilies "of a missionary nature," the decree states.
Father Andreassi explained the date was chosen with an eye to the feast of Christ the King (an observance also created by Pope Pius XI), which was initially celebrated on the last Sunday of October, ahead of All Saints' Day, to underscore the Church's missionary task ahead of Christ's return. (Later, Pope Paul VI sought to highlight the eschatological dimensions of the Christ the King feast by making it the final Sunday of the liturgical year, immediately before the First Sunday of Advent.)
At first, the collection for World Mission Sunday was taken up in January, connecting the donations with the gifts brought by the Magi at Epiphany, said Father Andreassi, noting the mission collection was later moved to the actual observance in October.
Donations to the collection serve as the primary financial support for the Pontifical Mission Societies, a worldwide network operating at the service of the pope and consisting of four organizations designated as pontifical by Pope Pius XI in 1922.
The Society for the Propagation of the Faith supports the evangelization efforts of the local church; the Missionary Childhood Association educates children about their part in the church’s missionary outreach; the Society of St. Peter the Apostle trains the next generation of missionary clergy and consecrated religious; and the Pontifical Missionary Union focuses on forming clergy, religious and pastoral leaders more deeply in their role as evangelizers.
In 2025, donations from Catholics in the U.S. alone enabled the societies to provide more than $30 million to build churches, convents, orphanages and schools; fund catechetical projects; and support dioceses, seminarians, and men and women religious.
With 1,130 mission territories worldwide, "each gets a relatively small amount of money" through a "very collaborative process" of allocation, said Father Andreassi.
And, he said, "Even in the mission lands, even if they may be a recipient (of mission funds), they take up a collection."
World Mission Sunday is "very much seen" as a day of "solidarity," one on which the Church recognizes that "we are all in this together," said Father Andreassi.
In contrast to that message of solidarity, World Mission Sunday surprisingly traces its roots in part to one of the most devastating conflicts in human history: the First World War.
That war "had dealt a serious blow to the missions, reducing the number of missionaries and disrupting many of the schools, hospitals, and charitable institutions they maintained," Father Andreassi told OSV News, quoting from his original research on the history of World Mission Sunday.
In his 1919 apostolic letter "Maximum Illud," Pope Benedict XV urged the Church to "rebuild and reinvigorate its missionary efforts," said Father Andreassi.
But after a war that felled no less than four empires -- Austro-Hungarian, German, Ottoman and Russian -- Pope Benedict XV realized "you don't just go back to doing what you used to be doing," Father Andreassi said.
Instead, the pope placed "renewed emphasis -- and in some places, emphasis for the first time -- on growing a native clergy (in various nations), so that all the priests were not just from the Netherlands and England and Ireland," Father Andreassi said.
In so doing, Pope Benedict strove to "free Catholic missionary activity from excessive identification with European nationalism and colonial interests," said the priest. "At the same time, he sought to enlist the entire Catholic world in the missionary enterprise through prayer, missionary vocations, and financial support."
Those efforts "exploded" when then-Msgr. ─ later Bishop, and now Blessed ─ Fulton J. Sheen was appointed the U.S. director of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith in 1950, said Father Andreassi.
A pioneer in Catholic communications with an already developed national audience, Blessed Sheen was able to place his popularity in service of the missions, said the priest.
"Now you're starting to see Sheen on local television stations talking about World Mission Sunday," said Father Andreassi. "You're seeing offers in anticipation of World Mission Sunday -- if you send a few dollars to the national office, you'll get a World Mission Rosary. So now World Mission Sunday is now becoming a huge event. There were a lot of things happening (on behalf of the missions), but he brought them up ten levels."
The impact of Blessed Sheen "then had ripple effects on the diocesan offices" of the mission societies, the priest added.
Ahead of this year's World Mission Sunday, the Pontifical Mission Societies have garnered increased attention with the recent beatification of the prelate in St. Louis.
Father Andreassi noted that as Blessed Sheen expanded the profile of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith during his 16-year tenure as national director, the Church was invigorating the mission field throughout the latter 20th century by sending priests to minister in other nations and to help animate local vocations.
He cited the Fidei Donum ("gift of faith") priests, diocesan clergy assigned to foreign missions.
"Historically, if you became a priest of the Diocese of Pittsburgh, you were going to work in Pittsburgh, with some rare exceptions," said Father Andreassi, noting that while "many religious orders already had a missionary arm to them," the commitment of diocesan clergy to missions marked a shift.
Other inflection points in more recent years have included the COVID-19 pandemic, after which "national and the diocesan offices have really been tapping into new media to get the word out like it's never been done before," he said.
Another challenge is simply "trying to get the attention of Catholics," since "so many things are pulling at our attention," Father Andreassi said.
But missionary outreach is "central to the life of the Christian," even in places where the Church is seemingly well grounded ─ including the U.S., where "many things" still "challenge or threaten the faith," he said.
Missionary efforts must "lead to an interior transformation," said Father Andreassi. "We're looking to convert hearts and minds."
- - - Gina Christian is a multimedia reporter for OSV News. Follow her on X @GinaJesseReina.

articles.title_orig: Privacy watchdog launches probe into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
articles.title_zh: Privacy watchdog launches probe into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
articles.content_orig:
Commissioner said Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The Australian privacy regulator has opened an investigation into the China-based software company behind the HeyCyan app in Kmart’s $89 smartglasses, following public outrage over the covert use of the devices.
In August, Guardian Australia reported Kmart had sold out of the Anko-branded discount version of Meta’s smartglasses that can capture images and record high-definition video, which led to widespread concern and calls to ban or restrict their use.
A GetUp petition has had more than 55,000 signatures calling to restrict the use of what has been labelled as “pervert glasses”, and councils around the country have looked to ban the glasses in public spaces such as swimming pools. The federal government is also considering a restriction on use in government workplaces.
The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses at the time.
Kind wrote to Kmart and BDI Technology, retailers for the glasses, as well as Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the glasses. She also wrote to Meta – for its Ray-Bans glasses – and Google which is planning its own smartglasses.
In a blog post on Wednesday , Kind announced an investigation has been opened into Shenzhen Qingcheng after it failed to respond to inquiries, “as well as concerns arising from third party analysis of the technology itself as well as the entity’s privacy policy”
None of the other companies will be investigated as part of this process, Kind said.
The privacy commissioner also highlighted the difficulty in applying privacy law to individuals who may use the devices given the privacy act only applies to companies and Commonwealth agencies – not individuals.
“Retailers that sell smart glasses – for example on an e-commerce website – or companies that manufacture them, may not have any Privacy Act obligations if they do not collect any personal information with respect to those devices,” Kind said.
“Instead, the entity providing the software at use in the device is likely to be the entity that collects and holds the information for the purpose of privacy law.”
Kind said that potential changes to the privacy act proposed by the government would strengthen how privacy law would apply to surveillance wearables such as smartglasses.
“The most substantial change will be the replacement of the ‘reasonably necessary for an entity’s functions and activities’ test with a ‘fair and reasonable’ test,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
“The new test will require an entity to look at a range of factors, including the extent to which an individual had genuine choice in the collection of their personal information, as well as the best interests of the child where children are involved.”
Kind said she hoped the community would “find comfort” in the proposed reforms as it would raise the bar over what personal information smartglasses can collect.
“These reforms are likely to become increasingly necessary as we face subsequent generations of surveillance wearables and connected devices, from personal assistant gadgets to ambient recording badges.”
Researchers at the University of Sydney in August analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.
In a subset of these videos, about 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage.
Canterbury-Bankstown and Sydney City are among the councils in Sydney to have banned the glasses from some venues, as well as Brisbane in Queensland, and Yarra city council in Melbourne.
Shenzhen Qingcheng was approached for comment.

articles.title_orig: Crypto megadonors play it safe in the House
articles.title_zh: Crypto megadonors play it safe in the House
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency's biggest political spending network is making its first broad push into general-election House races this cycle, saying it plans to back 32 incumbents in hopes of preserving a pro-crypto bloc in Congress .
Fairshake and its affiliated super political action committees announced Monday that they have committed funds to support 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats who have supported the crypto industry's priorities.
The spending plan comes less than a month before November's midterm elections , which will determine which party controls the House and Senate.
"Fairshake has always been and always will be an issue-focused organization," spokesperson Geoff Vetter said in a statement on Monday. "We back pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties."
The network is committing at least $1 million in support of six House incumbents: Democratic Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Steven Horsford of Nevada; and Derek Tran of California; and Republicans French Hill of Arkansas , Bill Huizenga of Michigan; and Bryan Steil of Wisconsin .
Fairshake did not disclose how much the super PAC network plans to spend on the other 26 candidates.
But the network, whose backers include Coinbase, Ripple, and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz , has ample financial firepower.
Fairshake and its two affiliated super PACs, Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, entered September with about $120.4 million in cash, according to Federal Election Commission filings . Protect Progress generally supports Democrats, and Defend American Jobs generally supports Republicans.
Fairshake's network earlier this election cycle spent $71 million across 57 primaries and special elections. Its preferred candidates won 53 races.
The new general-election spending push comes weeks after the CLARITY Act , the crypto industry's signature market-structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate. That leaves the industry's biggest legislative priority unresolved, and means the next Congress could determine how crypto is regulated in the U.S.
Crypto companies back the bill because it would set clearer rules for issuing and trading tokens, shift oversight of many digital assets from the Securities and Exchange Commission to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , and reduce the risk of securities-law enforcement.
All 32 candidates whom Fairshake is backing voted for the CLARITY Act when it passed the House 294-134 in July 2025.
Several of Fairshake's biggest beneficiaries are positioned to influence how that bill is handled in the next Congress. Hill and Huizenga are, respectively, the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, while Steil leads its digital-assets subcommittee.
On the Republican side, Fairshake is backing Ben Cline in Virginia ; Troy Downing in Montana ; Tom Emmer and Michelle Fischbach in Minnesota ; Scott Fitzgerald and Bryan Steil in Wisconsin ; Mike Haridopolos in Florida ; Pat Harrigan and David Rouzer in North Carolina ; French Hill in Arkansas ; Bill Huizenga and Lisa McClain in Michigan ; Brian Jack and Austin Scott in Georgia ; Frank Lucas in Oklahoma ; August Pfluger in Texas ; Guy Reschenthaler and G.T. Thompson in Pennsylvania ; and Jason Smith in Missouri .
Its Democratic slate includes California Reps. Pete Aguilar, Jimmy Panetta and Derek Tran; Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania ; Janelle Bynum of Oregon ; Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey ; Steven Horsford of Nevada ; Jonathan Jackson of Illinois ; Lucy McBath of Georgia ; Sarah McBride of Delaware ; Hillary Scholten of Michigan ; Terri Sewell of Alabama ; and Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia .
Fairshake this cycle has already spent nearly $30 million in hopes of defeating Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown in Ohio.
Fairshake spent about $40 million to defeat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill.

articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran-backed Houthis deny losing ground in Yemen as oil prices ease despite fierce fighting
articles.content_orig:
A U.S.-run military air base in England faced Iranian-related threats, and the Trump administration believes the intention was to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible, a U.S. official told The Associated Press.
The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity, could not speak to the nature of the potential attack. The United States removed its bombers from RAF Fairford , located 100 miles west of London, which has been used by American planes to strike Iran during this year's war.
President Trump told reporters on Monday he didn't want to tempt "the enemy" by having the bombers there.
The new details come as British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old British man in central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. He is the seventh person arrested in connection with the suspected plot against RAF Fairford, which authorities have linked to Iran. But British police so far have released few details of their investigation.
Six of the men arrested have since been released on bail, which drew criticism from Mr. Trump last week .
Iran summoned French ambassador to Tehran, Pierre Cochard, on Tuesday over Paris's treatment of protesters demanding better conditions in schools, state media reported, with French police having clashed for days with demonstrators.
Iran accused France of "violent treatment" of the protesters and "extensive and flagrant human rights violations" during the demonstrations, which began late last month and have been accompanied by unrest.
Relations between France and Iran have been strained for months, with the two expelling each other's diplomats in August.
Iran itself suffered major anti-government protests in January, during which the authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, blaming "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs maintain that security forces fired on protesters.
Most families of the six soldiers killed in the deadliest attack of the Iran war will not be attending a major White House event for Gold Star families hosted by President Trump.
Only one family member of those killed in an Iranian drone strike March 1 on Port Shuaiba in Kuwait confirmed to The Associated Press that they planned to attend Tuesday's reception with Mr. Trump and the first lady.
"There are questions about what happened before the attack, what information was available, what decisions were made, and what happened in the moments leading up to six American soldiers losing their lives," Joey Amor — whose 39-year-old wife, Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor , was among those killed — said in a public Facebook statement Monday. "I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency."
Some Gold Star families say they are grateful for how the Trump administration and military have honored their loved one's sacrifice. Other families say the way the White House has handled the reception is the latest indication that the administration does not respect the price they have paid.
The spouse of Maj. Alex Klinner, an airman who was killed in an Iran-related combat operation this summer, said receiving less than two weeks' notice did not give her enough time to arrange for overnight care for her three young children.
In a text message, Libby Klinner said she would not have gone anyway, adding, "I have no interest in supporting an administration that has been so reckless with the lives of our service members."
The war, launched Feb. 28, has claimed the lives of 19 U.S. troops and wounded more than 800 others.
The Houthis were fighting Tuesday around Dhubab, a strategic town in Yemen that its internationally-recognized government had previously said it had retaken, a senior Yemeni military official told The Associated Press. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.
Joined by its Yemeni government allies, Saudi Arabia is leading a coalition to attack Houthi military targets in Yemen. Their offensive follows the government's announcement on Sunday, declaring a campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territories in the country. Fighting has been concentrated in a region near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil and gas exports.
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said on Tuesday that its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at a city in Saudi Arabia's southwest.
The coalition's spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said on X that it "intercepted and destroyed" the missile launched towards Khamis Mushait, which is home to an air base.
U.S. military officials on Tuesday denied Iranian state media's reports of a downed U.S. Navy helicopter in the Red Sea.
"Iranian state media has been pushing false reports that a U.S. Navy MH-60R helicopter crashed in the Red Sea after declaring an emergency last night," U.S. Central Command wrote in a post on X .
CENTCOM said the reports were "not true" and that "all U.S. military aircraft and personnel across the Middle East are safe and unaccounted for."
Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, dismissed U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's latest statements on Iran, calling his forecasts "delusional" and accusing Washington of propaganda.
"Bessent's delusional forecasts never had any credibility in the first place. His latest propaganda will have an equally short shelf life," Rezaei wrote on X.
He added: "You lost the military war. You will fail in the economic war, too. Hormuz will not be opened by threats or pressure. Iran will not back down."
The White House on Tuesday denied that President Trump suggested Iran should "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego.
At a campaign rally in Nebraska, Mr. Trump called the Iran war "artificial," but added that he wanted to see a "total victory." He suggested the war was a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe."
"They can take out a city," Mr. Trump said, alluding to the risk of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego."
Attendees cheered after his remark. It was not immediately clear what Mr. Trump meant, but the comments were quickly condemned by California Gov. Gavin Newsom and other state officials.
White House spokesperson Steven Cheung posted Tuesday on X that "the media freakout" over Mr. Trump's remarks was "not rooted in reality."
"He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung argued. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."
Three Iranian men went on trial in the U.K. Tuesday on charges of spying for Iran, allegedly laying the groundwork for a violent attack against at least one London-based journalist.
The Iranian nationals visited addresses linked to people including two journalists working for the Farsi-language Iran International television network, which Tehran has long labeled a terror organization.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, who have all pleaded not guilty, appeared at a court in London accompanied by translators Tuesday.
Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones told the jury the three were accused of conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service, "in other words ... they spied on people of interest to the Iranian regime."
Another of the men's targets was lawyer Jonathan Turner, a founding member of the group U.K. Lawyers for Israel.
The three accused men do not deny visiting the addresses and taking photos and videos, but Sepahvand claimed he had been coerced and acted out of fear, the prosecution said.
Manesh and Noori said they were not aware that what they were doing was to assist the Iranian intelligence services, the prosecution added.

articles.title_orig: Germany arrests former intelligence chief in espionage case
articles.title_zh: Germany arrests former intelligence chief in espionage case
articles.content_orig:
August Hanning, the former president of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), appears as a witness before the NSA investigative committee at the German parliament Bundestag in Berlin on Oct. 1, 2015. Michael Kappeler/DPA via AP hide caption
BERLIN — A former head of Germany 's foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor's office said.
August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is "strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage," the federal prosecutor's office said in a statement.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
"In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service," Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor's office, told German broadcaster RTL later on Tuesday.
"In another instance, he is alleged to have passed on information following an extensive exchange — also with an employee of another intelligence service."
Neither Peterson nor the earlier statement by the prosecutor's office revealed who exactly the two men were suspected of spying for or which foreign intelligence services they provided with classified information.
Premises belonging to both men were searched Tuesday.
The prosecutor's office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning's chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
"In his role, he had access to confidential information," the prosecutor's office said.
Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings," the statement said.
Hanning used the information in private consulting work and Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information until June 2022, Peterson said.
Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block's children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.
The investigation into that case led to Tuesday's arrests.
The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning's residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor's office stated.
Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor's office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.
The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.
A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
"This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story," said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
"We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning," he told Spiegel Online.
"We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in Germany for years," he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.
