articles.title_orig: Cornell Faculty Senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell Faculty Senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty members introduced a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house.
The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday evening, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
“That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” says the resolution, which is less than half a page.
The measure is expected to be considered by the Faculty Senate, which meets Oct. 14, Faculty Senate member Paul Ortiz said in a statement.
Ortiz said in an interview: “My primary job as an educator is to make sure my students are studying and learning in a safe environment. If they don’t feel safe, they can’t learn, they can’t study, they can’t thrive, they can’t grow as individual human beings.”
Ortiz added that there is a “climate of fear among women students.” He emphasized that the Senate’s goal is to force “systemic change” rather than advocate to have one or two people, such as university President Michael Kotlikoff, step down.
You get “rid of one person, and then you bring a new person into a dysfunctional environment,” Ortiz said.
“A lot of the students would like the president to step down, but we decided not to have that in the resolution,” he added.
In a statement accompanying the resolution, the faculty sponsors said “numerous Cornell colleagues” had approached them demanding action, while students had told faculty members they were “upset [and] fearful for their personal safety” and wanted the Ivy League school to address sexual assault on campus.
Cornell alumni had also contacted faculty members and shared “their own traumatic stories as students,” the statement said.
Cornell declined to comment.
The proposed no-confidence resolution escalates the pressure on Cornell and its administration following national scrutiny over how the case was handled. Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with her allegation of sexual assault.
She alleges that multiple fraternity members sexually assaulted her in October 2024 while she was impaired by alcohol, ketamine and marijuana.
The woman’s allegations have made national headlines for days, and they prompted protests on campus following widespread criticism that the university and local officials did not do enough to investigate them.
Anne Marie Elizabeth Brady, a Faculty Senate member and research director for the university’s Industrial and Labor Relations Workers Institute, said the resolution came together “quickly” in recent days.
“If I was a woman on Cornell’s campus, I’d run in the other direction,” she said. “Because I’m not sure Cornell is there to protect the students the way they should be.”
Brady said Cornell’s decision to discipline the seven men accused of wrongdoing instead of passing the case on to outside law enforcement “feels like a cover-up to me.”
“If I’m a betting woman, I suspect they didn’t do that because they wanted to keep it secret,” she said. “They wanted to manage the story.”
If the Faculty Senate passes the resolution, Brady said, it will then prompt a series of discussions between faculty members and Cornell’s leadership for policies about sexual assault.
Similar action was taken last year following years of campus protests of the war in Gaza. Brady said those recommendations have largely been ignored.
“If the administration came out and said: ‘You know what? We screwed up, we did A, B and C wrong. We failed this student, we failed all our students through this process and these are the concrete ways and steps we are going to take to change,’” she said, “if they did that? That goes so far.”
Adam Reiss and Maggie Vespa reported from Ithaca and Matt Lavietes from New York City.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal
articles.title_zh: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal
articles.content_orig:
The Emmy Awards will leave its long-running broadcast network rotation for Amazon Prime Video in 2027 under a six-year exclusive global streaming deal, the e-commerce giant and the Television Academy announced on Tuesday.
Under the agreement, Prime Video will stream the annual awards honoring the best in TV for free to all audiences, including nonsubscribers, in more than 240 countries and territories.
Prime Video's rights to the Emmys will begin with the 2027 ceremony. NBC, owned by Comcast , aired the 2026 ceremony on Sept. 14.
Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior.
The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994 , with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year.
"Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement.
"Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year," he said.
The decision to move the 70-plus-year-old awards show to streaming reflects a broader trend in a shifting media landscape as Americans continue to ditch broadcast and cable TV for streaming service subscriptions. Streaming services have pushed further into live events in recent years, securing entertainment and sports rights alongside broadcast networks, and even winning rights that were previously exclusive to networks.
In December 2025, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal with Alphabet's YouTube and YouTube TV for media rights to the Oscars, taking over from ABC in 2029. Netflix has exclusively aired the SAG Awards since 2024.

articles.title_orig: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.title_zh: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.content_orig:
Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements
The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.
This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel .
The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.
Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.
The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.
The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem.
An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.
“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”
The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.
It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile.
The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.
Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute.
Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo.
after newsletter promotion
“We are all concerned because if this (closure of the consulate) goes ahead it would be an incredibly damaging precedent for the status of missions in Jerusalem, which are monitoring the status quo,” said one western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“It would be inconceivable for the British government to accept (the closure) because they don’t recognise the authority of the Israeli government over Jerusalem under international law. Particularly as Israel is taking this step over British measures which are simply applying international law.”
Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine , in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.
France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.
UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.
The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.

articles.title_orig: Arcadia surrogacy scandal: Guojon Xuan and Sylvia Zhang arrested on child abuse charges
articles.title_zh: Arcadia surrogacy scandal: Guojon Xuan and Sylvia Zhang arrested on child abuse charges
articles.content_orig:
ARCADIA, Calif. (KABC) -- Los Angeles County sheriff's deputies raided an Arcadia home on Tuesday morning and arrested a couple accused in a surrogacy scandal involving 21 child victims, authorities said.
Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan, the man and woman who housed the children and are at the center of the case , were taken into custody during a joint operation involving the sheriff's department and the FBI.
The couple pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations during their arraignment Tuesday afternoon. They are being held on a $20 million bail each.
According to prosecutors, the couple allegedly misled surrogates they paid to carry their children through their own surrogacy company. A criminal complaint lists 10 counts against the couple and 55 overt acts of conspiracy to commit child abuse.
Xuan's attorney, Mitchell Krems, released the following statement:
"My client is innocent. It is the nanny's wrongdoing who went on the run. He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family."
L.A. County District Attorney Nathan Hochman and Sheriff Robert Luna held a news conference after the arrests, where they outlined the disturbing allegations against the defendants and Hochman described the Arcadia mansion as "a house of horrors."
Prosecutors said the couple misrepresented their family circumstances to some surrogates, including how many children they already had.
The two-story home allegedly had 32 motion-activated surveillance cameras, allowing the defendants to monitor the children and nannies. Prosecutors allege young children were subjected to repeated physical punishment and abuse by nannies in so-called "learning centers."
Zhang and Xuan are accused of instructing nannies about physical discipline and told them not to leave visible marks on the children.
According to the D.A., prosecutors are asking for bail to be set at $100 million in the case, describing the couple as a flight risk.
The couple has been under scrutiny since last summer, when they were arrested on suspicion of felony child endangerment and later released without being charged.
A search warrant obtained by 7 On Your Side Investigates shows the investigation began after their then-2-month-old son suffered an apparent head injury.
According to investigators, the couple's nanny, Chunmei Li, was captured on security camera video holding the infant inside the home. The warrant states that footage shows the baby "cries for a few seconds until a thud or hit is heard," and that "crying suddenly stops." Police wrote that after Li's "attempt to wake him up" was "no success," the video shows Li "shake him."
Li remains at large, according to investigators.
Last summer, the 21 children found in the home were placed in the custody of the Los Angeles County Department of Children and Family Services.
The investigation determined that the children are the product of a surrogacy operation owned by Zhang and Xuan.
This is a developing story. This article will continue to be updated as more information becomes available.

articles.title_orig: FSU brings entrepreneurship educators from around the world to Tallahassee for training
articles.title_zh: FSU brings entrepreneurship educators from around the world to Tallahassee for training
articles.content_orig:
Home / News / FSU Global / FSU brings entrepreneurship educators from around the world to Tallahassee for training
Florida State University welcomed entrepreneu r ship educators and leaders from around the world to Tallahassee last month for the 26th Experiential Classroom , an intensive professional development program designed to strengthen entrepreneurship educat ion .
Hosted by FSU’s Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship , this year’s program took place Sept. 17-19 and brought together participants from six countries, 21 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, representing 58 institutions and organizations. International participants came to Tallahassee from Canada, Ecuador, the Dominican Republic, Armenia and India.
The Experiential Classroom is housed at FSU and offered in partnership with the University of Notre Dame , the University of Tampa and the University of Florida . It was founded in 1999 by Michael Morris, a faculty member of the McKenna Center for Human Development and Global Business in the Keough School of Global Affairs at the University of Notre Dame.
The program has become a leading professional development experience for faculty, doctoral students, program directors and others seeking to strengthen how they teach entrepreneurship.
“The reach of this year’s Experiential Classroom speaks to the global leadership role Florida State’s Jim Moran College plays in entrepreneurship education,” said Michael Brady, interim dean of the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship. “We want FSU to be a destination not only for students who want to study entrepreneurship, but also for educators from around the world who want to become better at teaching it.”
While most participants came from colleges and universities, the cohort also included representatives from a high school and school district, as well as and community organizations such as the Chicago Urban League, mHUB and the Chicago Community Trust.
Unlike a traditional academic conference, the Experiential Classroom operates as an immersive teaching clinic. Participants learn alongside experienced entrepreneurship educators through classroom demonstrations, interactive sessions and hands-on exercises they can adapt to their own classrooms and entrepreneurship programs.
“The Experiential Classroom is about learning how to teach entrepreneurship by experiencing great entrepreneurship education,” said Susana Santos, Jim Moran Associate Professor of Entrepreneurship and co-director of the program. “Bringing together educators with different disciplinary, institutional and cultural perspectives creates an incredible learning environment. Participants leave with practical approaches they can immediately put to work and a global network of colleagues to rely on long after the clinic ends.”
The Experiential Classroom is part of FSU’s broader work to strengthen entrepreneurship education in the United States and abroad.
In 2025, Santos and Eric Liguori, Jim Moran Professor and associate dean for research and external relations in the college, traveled to Armenia with Vilma Fuentes, a visiting associate in research at FSU’s Learning Systems Institute , to train more than 30 faculty and administrators at the Armenian State University of Economics (ASUE) on contemporary approaches to entrepreneurship education.
The training was part of a U.S. Department of State-funded partnership designed to strengthen STEM and social entrepreneurship education and educational ties between the United States and Armenia. Liguori also regularly leads entrepreneurship educator development programs at universities across the United States, extending FSU’s expertise in experiential entrepreneurship education to faculty and institutions beyond the university’s campuses.
FSU’s work to advance entrepreneurship education internationally is also expanding through a strategic partnership with Universal AI University in Mumbai, India. Through the partnership, FSU faculty are working with their counterparts in India to help integrate entrepreneurship education into the university’s curriculum, bringing together FSU’s expertise in entrepreneurship education with Universal AI University’s focus on artificial intelligence and emerging technology.
FSU’s role as a hub for entrepreneurship education will be on display again Oct. 15-17, when the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship hosts the 2026 Global Consortium of Entrepreneurship Centers Annual Conference, bringing hundreds of university entrepreneurship leaders, educators and ecosystem builders from around the world to Tallahassee.
For more information about conference registration and sponsorship opportunities, visit the conference’s webpage . To learn more about the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship, visit jimmorancollege.fsu.edu .
To learn more about FSU’s global footprint, visit global.fsu.edu .

articles.title_zh: TOP FIVE STORYLINES: Sheldon Haudenschild’s Homecoming Sends World of Outlaws to Three Ohio Ovals
articles.content_orig:
October 6, 2026 at 3:04 pm
Sheldon Haudenschild cares deeply for his Ohio roots and continuing the state’s rich Sprint Car racing tradition.
The Wooster, OH native’s passion will be on display this weekend as he’s bringing the World of Outlaws NOS Energy Drink Sprint Car Series to his home state for a tripleheader at three different racetracks. Sheldon Haudenschild ’s NOS Energy Drink Buckeye Brawl Weekend sets the stage for a big trip to the “Buckeye State.” All three races will dish out $18,000 to the winner, a nod to Haudenschild’s car number with KCP Racing.
The brawl begins at Findlay, OH’s Millstream Speedway on Thursday, Oct. 8. The tour returned last year for the first time since 1994 and is back for a second consecutive season.
Round two takes The Greatest Show on Dirt to Mansfield Speedway on Friday, Oct. 9. Matt Tift and his team revived the historic track and are ready to welcome the World of Outlaws for the first time in 45 years.
The “Buckeye State” showcase is finalized on Saturday, Oct. 10, at Hartford, OH’s Sharon Speedway as the World of Outlaws makes its 16th stop at the northeast Ohio facility.
Let’s look at the top stories to watch this week:
The KCP Racing pit area will be busy all three nights this week.
Sheldon Haudenschild has amassed one of the most passionate followings in the sport, and it’s felt nowhere more than when he comes home. The Ohio fans watched his dad Jac Haudenschild ride the Haud Line to 72 World of Outlaws victories and many more accolades, and they’ve watched Sheldon follow in his footsteps in carving out his own legacy. He’s up to 55 career wins with nine of them coming this year, his first campaign with the KCP team.
Haudenschild would love nothing more than to add to that total this week. He’s won before at Millstream, topping a 2016 All Star Circuit of Champions (ASCoC) visit. Friday will mark his debut at Mansfield. He bagged a Sharon trophy with ASCoC in 2015 at the Lou Blaney Memorial . In World of Outlaws competition, he’s finished on the podium in four of his six tries. Sheldon Haudenschild has had this weekend circled on his calendar all year (Tyler Carr Photo)
David Gravel is closing in on history.
A rough stretch in California for the two-time opened the door for Michael “Buddy” Kofoid ’s championship hopes, but Gravel did his best to shut it as the scene shifted east. A win and a fourth at Williams Grove Speedway ’s National Open upped his point lead to 142 with just 10 races remaining. If he can hold on, he’ll join Steve Kinser, Donny Schatz , and Brad Sweet as only the fourth driver to ever claim three consecutive titles.
Don’t expect Gravel to stumble on Thursday as he enters Millstream as the defending winner at the Findlay, OH track. The Watertown, CT will make his first Mansfield laps the next night. He and Big Game Motorsports have been stellar at Sharon with a 2.8 average finish in six tries, highlighted by a 2024 triumph.
A trio of California-born World of Outlaws competitors ( Buddy Kofoid , Carson Macedo , and Cole Macedo ) consider Ohio a home away from home and look forward to any swing through the state. All three are united in the Linder family providing them a place to stay as they expanded their racing careers eastward.
Kofoid sits second in the standings heading to Ohio during his third tour with Roth Motorsports. His Millstream debut a year ago resulted in a runner-up finish. The time with the Linders led him to making one prior appearance at Mansfield, a fourth-place effort in 2019. He’s made four Sharon appearances, peaking at second last year.
Carson Macedo resides fourth in points, a manageable 32 markers back of Sheldon Haudenschild for third. His three trips to Millstream yielded a best finish of ninth last year in the Jason Johnson Racing No. 41. The Lemoore, CA native owns more Mansfield experience than most of his fellow World of Outlaws drivers with five starts leading to three podiums, including a 2018 Sprint Car World Championship prelim score. None of Macedo’s 10 Sharon Feature starts have resulted in a win, but he’s been on the podium on four occasions.
Cole Macedo’s sophomore World of Outlaws season sees him sitting eighth in the standings, which would mark a two-spot improvement over his rookie campaign if he can stay there. He took the TwoC Racing ride from 14th to seventh at Millstream last year. He’ll get his first look at Mansfield Saturday. Last year in his seventh Sharon appearance, the 26-year-old started on the pole and finished a solid sixth.
And speaking of Cole Macedo , he leads the most hotly contested battle in the points. Spots eight through 12 are separated by only 120 markers. The point fund and exclusivity bonus pay $70,000 more to finish eighth over 12th, so the five drivers in this fight will be scratching and clawing for every point they can get.
Behind Macedo, next in line is Spencer Bayston as his first year with Stenhouse Jr./Marshall Racing winds down. He won the season opener and has piled up 32 top 10s. He trails Macedo by 62.
Then it’s leading Kevin Gobrecht Rookie of the Year presented by Five Star Bodies contender Emerson Axsom 16 markers back of Bayston. Axsom and the Klaasmeyer/Petry Motorsports team have found some speed over the last couple months with 13 top 10s in 17 races, highlighted by Axsom’s first World of Outlaws win at Huset’s Speedway.
Only two points behind Axsom is Bill Balog . The “North Pole Nightmare” has dealt with several cases of bad luck recently, but his speed over that time suggests it wouldn’t be a surprise at all if the No. 17B breaks through into Victory Lane soon.
Rounding out the group is Series sophomore Chris Windom with 40 markers separating him from Balog. He got his first career victory in August at I-55 and picked up a pair of podiums last month in the Sides Motorsports No. 7S. Cole Macedo leads a hotly contested battle for eighth in the standings into Ohio (Tyler Carr Photo)
The World of Outlaws will have a group of talented “Buckeyes” ready to brawl this week with hopes of battling the best of the best for wins on the sport’s biggest stage.
Dale Blaney may only show up at Sharon, but he’s likely to make the most of that appearance. Last year he wheeled his brother Dave’s No. 10 to an extremely popular win at their home track, becoming the oldest victor in Series history at 61 years old.
Bradner, OH’s Nate Dussel has won at both Mansfield and Sharon this year. He’s topped a pair of FAST races at Mansfield and beat the ASCoC at Sharon in August.
Bellevue, OH’s Cap Henry is always one to watch when the World of Outlaws roll into his local region. He’s won nine 410 Sprint Car races in 2026, including Mansfield’s season opener in May.
These three will be joined by plenty more local gassers looking to impress under the bright lights.

articles.title_orig: Toyota shuts down rumors claiming that it’s ‘slashing prices’ in China
articles.title_zh: Toyota shuts down rumors claiming that it’s ‘slashing prices’ in China
articles.content_orig:
Toyota’s joint venture, FAW Toyota, issued a statement denying reports that it’s “slashing prices” in China and may exit the market entirely.
Toyota sells vehicles in China through two joint ventures: FAW Toyota and GAC Toyota. The long-standing joint ventures produce and sell Toyota models, including the Corolla, RAV4, and Avalon, as well as new electric vehicles like the bZ3 and bZ5.
Last week, on September 28, GAC Group announced plans to acquire a 50% stake in FAW Toyota. The plans include issuing new A-shares priced at 5.75 yuan per share.
Under the agreement, GAC said that FAW Group would become its second-largest shareholder, but exact details would be finalized following an audit and once the valuation work was complete.
FAW Toyota was established in 2000 as a joint venture between FAW Group and Toyota, with each holding a 50% share. It was initially called Tianjin FAW Toyota Motor Co until 2003, when it adopted the name FAW Toyota.
Once the agreement is finalized, GAC Group would take FAW’s 50% stake, while Toyota would retain the other 50%. GAC said the deal would not change the controller.
The move was widely viewed as part of Toyota’s efforts to revamp slumping brand sales in China and streamline operations.
Since the announcement, several reports have claimed that FAW Toyota plans to exit the market completely and is slashing prices to sell down inventory.
FAW Toyota issued a statement on Monday night, refuting the false claims. The company said:
In response to false statements circulating on certain online platforms —such as claims that “FAW Toyota may completely exit the market” and “Toyota is slashing prices”—our company reserves the right to pursue legal action.
The joint venture added that “the production, sales, and iterative development plans for all models are progressing smoothly as scheduled.”
Looking ahead, FAW Toyota will leverage the Group’s broader resources and technology for upcoming vehicles.
Toyota’s sales in China fell by 22.8% in August, marking the seventh straight month of lower sales due to weak demand for gas and hybrid models amid soaring fuel prices.

articles.title_orig: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.title_zh: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.content_orig:
YANKTON, S.D. – Julie Jones won silver at the World Archery 3D Championships, and in doing so created history by becoming the first USA woman to win an individual medal at the event, which began in 2003.
Jones was making only her second-ever appearance at the World Archery 3D Championships. She was part of the women’s team including Jayme Buchanan, Katherine Li and Madison Ritter to claim bronze at the 2024 World 3D Championships in Mokrice, Slovenia. Two years on and she did even better.
“It's a little surreal, I'll be honest,” began Julie Jones on hearing she had made history. “I love 3D. That is my passion aside from hunting. I guess if you ask me how I felt about it, I'm glad that I could bring it back for the U.S. team. But it really isn't a short answer. It goes a lot further than that.
"This whole time that I've been shooting, I've had an incredible team of people behind me from the very beginning. They have encouraged, they've pushed, they've believed in me when I had doubts about my own abilities. Without them, none of none of this would have been possible.
“I know that I don't have to prove anything to them but bringing this silver medal home, it's a testament to the training and the coaching that that I've received, that this medal belongs to all of these people, not just to me.”
Jones was seeded seventh after qualification before moving through the bracket with wins over teammate Mandy Boggs, Olga Timofeeva (RUS) and Martina Blahusova (CZE). The U.S. archer from Texas settled for silver after defeat in the gold medal match to fifth seed Judith Wenzl (GER).
“I had 100 percent confidence in the training and the coaching that I'd received," explained Jones. "I knew that if I applied all of the mental work, all of the physical work, as well as the actual shooting, I was reasonably confident that I could be in the top 10. That really wasn't a doubt in my mind.
"I knew that if I ran my process and executed well, that there was a good chance I would be in the top five, if not the top three. So that part of it was not necessarily a surprise to me.
“I've had some health challenges along the way and so day two was not a good day for me physically. And it was a struggle just to make it through the round. So that kind of threw a spanner into it.
“But I'm glad that it worked out as well as it did. I shoot very well under pressure. And I knew that if I could make it into those head-to-head eliminations, that I could work. Even though I had dropped points on day two, I knew that I could work myself back up to a to a better position.”
Julie Jones was also part of the bronze medal-winning traditional mixed team alongside Cody Hasson. Hasson, a double gold medalist at last year’s Pan American Field Championships, finished sixth in the individual men’s event.
Jones added, “I am tickled to death that Cody and I ended up with the bronze medal. He is a really, really strong shooter. I may be mistaken, but I don't think he's ever medaled before (at World 3D), and just to see the excitement and the absolute joy on his and our coach Shiloh's (Butts) face, when we realized that we had won that last round, that was a great feeling.”
For Jones, this was a family affair, with husband Daniel having also made the team. For Daniel, it was not only his World 3D Championship debut but also his first major event outside of local competition. A first major event for Daniel and the first U.S. woman to win an individual medal at the World 3D Championships for Julie. A case of keeping up with the Joneses!
“I'm just a normal person,” continued Julie. “I'm a mom. I have kids. I'm self-employed. I don't have a big, fancy facility, but, you know, I go out and I'm passionate about 3D archery.”
This success comes just a few weeks before a significant birthday for Julie on November 1. She said with a smile, “Just a month before, to achieve this, I couldn’t ask for anything more. This is year 50 for me. I have my 50th birthday coming up. And winning individual silver is pretty much the best present that I could imagine.”
Matt Hudson and Ava Jones combined to take silver in the barebow mixed team. Seeded at number two, the pair defeated Austria (150-136) and Denmark (152-141) before defeat to Russia (144-123). Ava Jones, making her World Archery 3D Championships debut, came in fourth in barebow women.
Other top 10 individual finishes came for Kim Timberlake (4th in longbow women), Joella Bates (8th in longbow women) and Lee Wilkins (10th in longbow men). Timberlake’s march to the bronze medal match included a 96-66 quarterfinals win over third seed Paula Virmasalo (FIN).

articles.title_orig: New York declares state disaster emergency over rising measles cases. Here's what that means - ABC News
articles.title_zh: New York declares state disaster emergency over rising measles cases. Here's what that means - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
New York has recorded 108 measles cases so far this year, most since mid-July.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency on Monday as neighboring Pennsylvania battles its largest measles outbreak in three decades.
As of Oct. 3, New York has recorded 108 measles cases so far this year, 92 of those since mid-July across 18 rural counties where communities are under-immunized, according to Hochul's order.
"After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a state disaster emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Hochul said in a statement . "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease."
It marks the first time a state has issued an emergency order since measles cases began rising last year. At least 95% of measles cases in the U.S. have been among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown.
The order allows registered nurses to order the collection and testing of specimens for suspected measles cases.
Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 Fahrenheit and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek.
Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says.
The order, in effect until Nov. 4, allows pharmacists in New York to vaccinate ⁠children as young as age 2 with the MMR shot. It also expands who can administer MMR vaccines to include emergency medical technicians-paramedics, advanced EMS and midwives.
Additionally, it suspends a previous requirement that health care professionals who administer vaccines to those aged 19 and older receive consent before reporting vaccination to New York City or New York State immunizations registries. All MMR vaccinations of children and adults must be reported within 72 hours.
"Department staff are working closely with local health departments and regional partners to track and contain the current measles outbreak," Dr. James McDonald, commissioner for the New York State Department, said in a statement. "The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is the best protection -- protecting nearly all people against disease who receive the recommended doses."
The state said it has administered more than 1,000 MMR shots in rural areas since July.
Meanwhile, Pennsylvania health officials are now reporting more than 1,000 measles cases. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and the state has reported five measles-associated deaths, which is the most any state has reported in over 30 years.
This outbreak follows a trend of growing outbreaks in the U.S. over the last two years.
Earlier this year, South Carolina reported the end to a measles outbreak of 997 cases. Last year, Texas reported an outbreak of 762 cases.
Nationally, nearly 4,000 cases have been confirmed this year in the U.S., with infections reported in almost every state, according to the CDC . It's the highest number of illnesses from measles since 1991.
The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.
Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine.
However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.
School vaccine exemptions also reached a record high last school year. Recent CDC data showed that vaccine exemptions for kindergarteners increased to 4.2% during the 2025-26 school year. This is up from 3.6% compared to the previous school year and 2.2% during the 2020-21 school year.

articles.content_orig:
Musician Jack White has fired back at Donald Trump following the president’s remarks made that Iran could “take out Los Angeles” and “San Diego” while speaking about the international conflict on Monday at a rally in Nebraska.
“Hey republicans and conservatives that live in L.A. and San Diego; how do you feel about your Fuhrer recommending that the cities you live in get attacked? Click the video I reposted and watch for yourself,” White shared on Instagram Tuesday. “Listen to the cult members CLAPPING and cheering for this. Let me take a wild guess: it was a joke, owning the libs, insert cult rhetoric here, etc. The allegiance these people have to this corrupt felon is so laughable and ignorant.”
He continued: “That’s right, a U.S. ‘President’ that recommended that two major cities in our country be bombed because they don’t give total allegiance to his ego. Imagine any other President or elected official in history saying this. False flag incoming anyone? Just wait till next month when he begins enacting illegal measures to not allow democracy at the polls to prevail when the right lose badly in the mid term elections. I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again: The Worst American of All Time. #TWAAT ”
While onstage, Trump said that raising prices, due to the war, were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. “They can take out a city,” Trump continued. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.”
White has long opposed Trump and has blasted the president many times before. In Aug. 2025, the “White Stripes” vocalist took to social media to call him a danger “not just to America but the entire world and that’s not an exaggeration,” and in Feb., mocked Trump’s appearance and track record of international conflict, writing, “Behold the leader of the ‘Board of Peace.’ For the next war announcement donny, may I suggest having your feet up on the Resolute desk while eating a Big Mac in a velvet track suit?”
Gov. Gavin Newsom also spoke out after Trump’s comments, sharing several posts on X . “He is deranged and dangerous,” Newsom wrote in one post. “An American president is talking about Los Angeles and San Diego being ‘taken out.’ Where the hell is Congress? This is dangerous. The time to stand up is NOW,” he wrote in another.

articles.title_zh: Flu season could kick off ‘incredibly’ early — what scientists are watching
articles.content_orig:

            and JavaScript.
A variant of the H1N1 influenza virus is dominating flu season in the Northern Hemisphere so far this year. Shown here are H1N1 influenza virus particles (yellow) releasing from an infected lung cell (green). Credit: Science Photo Library
Data show that flu season in the Northern Hemisphere might be off to an early start — prompting a rethink about when people should get their annual vaccines against the influenza virus . The percentage of positive tests for influenza is unusually high for this time of the year in places such as the United Kingdom and on the West Coast of the United States (see ‘Surprising start’). In Japan, outbreaks in August and early September forced some schools to close just as they were starting back up after the summer break.
“It would be an incredibly early season” for the United States if the cases researchers are seeing on the West Coast continue to rise at their current rate, says Scott Hensley, a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.
The influenza subtype responsible for most of the US cases so far is H1N1, in a flip from last year, when H3N2 dominated. And sequencing data from these early cases point to an emerging mutation in H1N1 that is causing concern among specialists.
Source: Adapted from US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data
These findings come from a relatively small number of positive tests compared with those available during peak flu season, so it’s too soon to predict the overall trajectory of the outbreak, researchers say. “An early start doesn’t necessarily mean a more severe season,” says James Hay, an epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, UK. Still, “there is something afoot”, wrote epidemiologist Caitlin Rivers in her newsletter, ‘Force of Infection’, on 27 September .
It’s enough to make Rivers, who is a researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, reconsider her personal protection strategy. In a typical year, when flu season peaks in December and January in the United States, she would wait until mid-to-late October for a shot, to get the best protection. Now, she’s thinking about getting a jab as soon as possible.
Seasonal flu is usually caused by some combination of three viruses: two subtypes of influenza A — H3N2 and H1N1 — and influenza B. Because influenza viruses genetically mutate over time and people’s immunity alters as they get vaccines and infections, which of the three viruses emerges as dominant changes for each flu season. US data showed that, during the week ending on 26 September, H1N1 accounted for 96% of positive cases for which subtyping was performed. H3N2 accounted for almost 4% of cases, and influenza B wasn’t detected.
That’s in contrast to last year, when a new variant of H3N2, called subclade K, emerged. It became globally dominant because it had many mutations that made people more vulnerable to it.
Will the mRNA flu shot work better than a regular seasonal one? What the science says
Will the mRNA flu shot work better than a regular seasonal one? What the science says
This year, the H1N1 mutation that is worrying researchers is G155E. Alex Greninger, a virologist at the University of Washington in Seattle, says that his laboratory detected G155E in 13 of 17 H1N1 samples taken from people in whom the genetic sequences were complete enough to identify specific mutations. The samples had come from hospitals and clinics in Seattle over the past few months.
This mutation had already been flagged in an analysis led by Jesse Bloom, a virologist at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, which was posted on the preprint server bioRxiv last month, ahead of peer review 1 .
Bloom and his colleagues tested how well antibodies in blood samples from 260 people in Australia and the United States were able to recognize and block infection from 148 influenza A viruses circulating by mid-2026. “We saw that a number of strains which have the G155E mutation are, in some cases, less well recognized by pre-existing human antibodies,” Bloom says. Antibodies in serum from teenagers and young adults were especially inept at recognizing this variant, probably because many in these groups haven’t been exposed to H1N1 viruses with similar characteristics before .

articles.title_orig: Liberal justices look for 'escape hatch' as high-stakes climate case lands at Supreme Court, experts say
articles.title_zh: Liberal justices look for 'escape hatch' as high-stakes climate case lands at Supreme Court, experts say
articles.content_orig:
Utah and Alabama attorneys general warn Colorado’s climate case could drive up costs nationwide, while former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee argues Americans harmed by climate change deserve their day in court.
Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor's repeated questions concerning whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear a high-profile climate case that could expose oil companies to lawsuits across the country steered conservative lawyers to believe that the liberal justices are seeking an "off-ramp."
"The fact that they kept going back to trying to create a jurisdictional problem tells me they don't feel confident that they have the votes in this space," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, a conservative judicial group, told Fox News Digital. "Jackson and Sotomayor were looking for an escape hatch."
The Supreme Court began its new term Monday, hearing its first oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder, in which they will rule on whether state tort laws can be used to seek damages from oil companies for climate change, even when the alleged harms are occurring outside the state or continent. The justices will also rule on whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear this case now, as the case is still before the Colorado Supreme Court .
The case before the high court is in an unusual procedural posture, meaning the justices could resolve it without ever reaching the blockbuster state-versus-federal power fight at its center. That dispute centers on whether Colorado can use its own laws to seek damages for alleged harms caused by emissions from other states or whether it's an issue for the federal government and Congress to regulate.
Climate activist protesters gather outside the Supreme Court before oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder on Oct. 5, 2025. (Elaine Mallon/Fox News Digital)
SUPREME COURT BEGINS NEW TERM WITH HIGH-PROFILE LOOK AT CLEAN AIR AND FEDERAL AUTHORITY
"The questions by Jackson and Sotomayor trying to say it would be premature for the court to issue an opinion are simply the liberal justices trying to find an off-ramp for the case because they are afraid they will be outvoted on the main issue: does federal law such as the Clean Air Act preempt all state claims like those asserted here," Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital.
While questioning Suncor attorney Kannon Shanmugam, Jackson suggested the dispute may have reached the Supreme Court too soon, calling it "premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction."
She also repeatedly questioned why the court couldn't wait to hear the case, saying the court doesn't "have the whole set of facts" and that the court doesn't "really know enough to be confident" that the theories posed are applicable.
"It feels to me like the defendants ... are bringing it back to federal court before the state courts have really had a chance to sort out who is the source, what is their allegation with respect to how this causation is happening," Jackson told Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who argued in support of Suncor.
Meanwhile, Sotomayor refused to drop her line of questioning on jurisdiction with Shanmugam, proposing that the Supreme Court send the case back to the Colorado Supreme Court.
"If we're unsure of your characterization, because there's certainly a number of amici brief who disagree with that characterization, shouldn't we be certifying this question to the Colorado court instead of us deciding it? We have to be sure of our jurisdiction before we take it," Sotomayor said.
Republican Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall told Fox News Digital it was clear that the liberal justices were trying to cast doubt on whether they have jurisdiction.
Climate activists gather outside the Supreme Court for oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder on Oct. 5, 2026. (Elaine Mallon/Fox News Digital)
SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA
"Well, I think you saw both Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor try to find an out for this court, basically saying the court doesn't have jurisdiction at this stage of the case to be able to make a final ruling. I think that you saw the advocates on behalf of Suncor be able to distinguish that."
If the Supreme Court declines to reach the federalism issue, the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing Boulder's state-law claims to proceed would remain in place, leaving the broader question of how far states can use tort law to pursue climate claims against energy companies unresolved.
Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Boulder attorney Kevin Russell on whether a Boulder win could trigger similar lawsuits nationwide. Russell said there are legal limits, but acknowledged to Justice Clarence Thomas that Boulder's theory could allow other fossil-fuel businesses to be sued.
"The chief justice and the court do not like issuing rulings with no limiting principles, rulings that could open up unlimited litigation and claims. Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer for Suncor, emphasized this again at the very end of the oral argument when he pointed out that there are not only 90,000 political jurisdictions that could sue, but individuals could also sue claiming damages from global warming," von Spakovsky said.
"And he also pointed out something the conservative majority frowns upon: that Boulder is trying to resolve a major policy issue in the courts instead of in the legislative branches," von Spakovsky continued.
Conservative lawyers believe that Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor are seeking an "off-ramp." (Getty Images)
SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE
Supporters of Suncor say the lawsuits could "bankrupt" oil companies and cause the price for consumers to go up.
"It's to basically create a carbon tax on both producers and emitters across the country, which would include, by the way, my cattlemen in Alabama producing beef for our country, those that are creating concrete to be able to build structures and be able to grow our economy," Marshall told Fox News. "They ultimately want to bankrupt that industry to have their preferred climate change policies be in play."
"They're literally addressing behavior that takes place all over the world," Utah Attorney General Derek Brown told Fox News Digital. "They want to regulate not just what happens in Colorado, but what happens in my state of Utah or in Saudi Arabia. That's not the way the system works. So, really, this case comes down to one main issue and that is who gets to decide things like energy policy. And ultimately, under our system, it should be Congress."
Meanwhile, Boulder alleged ExxonMobil and Suncor knew for decades about the climate risks associated with fossil fuels but misled the public about those risks. The communities estimate that taxpayers could face more than $100 million in costs to adapt to climate-related impacts, including wildfires, drought and damage to roads and other infrastructure.
Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat and longtime advocate for aggressive action on climate change, argued those costs are already being felt by communities across the country.
"As governor, I've worked with so many families who've lost their homes," Inslee told Fox News Digital. "So many communities have essentially burned down, and they ought to be able to have a day in court to hear the evidence, to determine whether the lies of the oil and gas industry legitimately, they make it so that they're held accountable."
The complaint pointed to a 1977 internal memo from ExxonMobil that circulated among the company's highest-level managers. The memo reported that "current scientific opinion overwhelmingly favors" that fossil fuels contribute to the rise in CO2 emissions.

articles.title_orig: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.title_zh: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.content_orig:
White House denies the allegations as ‘false’ and says ‘first amendment does not protect violent rioting’
US politics live – latest updates
Donald Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint.
Alex Padilla, a Democratic senator who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of the complaint, which makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025.
Demonstrators had been protesting against Trump’s deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to push the president’s agenda.
“These allegations are deeply alarming,” Padilla, who also serves as the top Democrat on the border security and immigration subcommittee, said in a statement. “Using the FBI to target Americans for exercising their first amendment rights directly undermines our nation’s foundational values. I won’t rest until we get answers.”
NBC first reported on the allegations after viewing a copy of the disclosure, which identifies the whistleblower as Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, who made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE protests around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, in February last year.
Fields alleges that Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told Akil Davis, the head of the field office, to open an investigation into protesters’ activities outside federal buildings, even though Fields says the demonstrations were protected free speech, and several FBI employees expressed concern with the legality of these requests.
Field, who joined the FBI in May 2016, also alleges that Trump reportedly viewed a TikTok video of protesters in Alhambra, California, that alerted neighbors about the presence of federal immigration officers and advised them of their legal rights. The White House, Fields says, then instructed Patel to direct the Los Angeles field office to initiate an investigation into those demonstrating in the video, because the president “was angry about the incident”.
Despite the fact that member of Fields’s team determined that the protesters’ actions were constitutionally protected and there was insufficient evidence, Fields was told by a colleague – whose name is redacted – that “the president wants this investigation”. Fields says that even though her supervisor acknowledged the investigation was unconstitutional, the directive still had to be followed.
Fields alleges that a “dedicated immigration squad” was created, comprising 10 agents, some of whom were taken off active cartel cases to carry out the White House’s requests. Fields says that she questioned the directives “operational logic” but her supervisor – whose name is also redacted in the complaint – described the move as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president”.
Fields says, however, she was not aware of any “actual or potential national security threat, federal criminal activity, or vulnerability” that would have warranted conducting assessments or opening investigations into anti-ICE and CBP protesters at the time.
She ultimately resigned from the bureau last year after she was removed from overseeing several programs, and believes that her diminished role was the result of objecting to protest-related investigations, according to the complaint.
after newsletter promotion
A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, called the allegations “false” in a statement to the Guardian. “The first amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” she said. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
Meanwhile, the FBI and justice department said in a joint statement they would “continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law”.
“The DoJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law. Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job,” they added.
In a letter to attorney general Todd Blanche and Patel, Padilla outlined Fields’s allegations and asked the officials dozens of questions about the reported investigations – including whether they resulted in arrests, how many directives of this kind the justice department has received from the president and the number of investigations that are still open.

articles.title_orig: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.title_zh: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.content_orig:
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.
"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."
"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
Students chant slogans during a demonstration against under-resourced schools, in Paris, Tuesday. Teresa Suarez/AP hide caption
The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.

articles.title_orig: They told the world AI was dangerous. Now Trump’s allies are coming for them.
articles.title_zh: They told the world AI was dangerous. Now Trump’s allies are coming for them.
articles.content_orig:
BERKELEY, Calif. - After artificial intelligence safety advocates captured Washington's attention with dire warnings about the technology's power, the Trump administration and its allies embraced some of their suggestions, while moving to sideline the advocates themselves.
Battle lines have been drawn in recent days over part of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI chief executives last week: Who should audit AI companies' systems to ensure their technology behaves as intended.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.
Leading AI companies - including OpenAI and Anthropic - have for years worked with a cluster of nonprofits concentrated in the Bay Area's AI safety community, which grew out of the effective altruism movement. But Trump's tech-world allies say the work of auditing AI should be taken on by America's largest consulting firms.
"In my view they should be professional auditors, not these NGOs," investor and former top White House AI adviser David Sacks said on his All-In podcast last week. He said in a post on X last month that the AI safety nonprofit METR, which has worked with Anthropic, was too close to the company to be called independent. Soon after, Anthropic said it would partner with consulting giant Accenture to build a team of outside evaluators.
At a conference here over the weekend, members of AI safety organizations grappled with the impact of what some see as a coordinated campaign to delegitimize their work and paint their community as cultish and unserious. The event took place at a former hotel popular with AI safety acolytes that also recently hosted a conference on AI consciousness and a sex workshop called "Slutcon."
Trump officials and allies have sniped at the movement for months but the attacks intensified after public anxiety over AI risks forced the White House to respond. Sacks last month shared on X a New York Post front page that called employees of METR, which helped OpenAI investigate its rogue AI agents, "THE WOKE WIZARDS OF AI." (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)
Trump on Sunday named several figures who have rejected calls from advocates for an AI industry-wide slowdown to his Super Intelligence Force advisory panel. They include Sacks and Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, who said last month that calls for action to prevent extreme scenarios of AI causing harm promoted "extinction, death-cult-like philosophies."
"There has absolutely been a rhetorical push within certain corners of the White House and broader Trump administration to get the message out about effective altruism and its potential dangers," said a Trump administration official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private discussions.
A White House official said that it supports organizations that evaluate the security and safety of how AI models are engineered. The official pointed to Trump's 2025 executive order targeting what the president termed "woke AI."
Anthropic declined to comment.
Nathan Leamer, director of the pro-industry nonprofit Build American AI, said he has been briefing congressional staff and other influential conservative figures in Washington about effective altruism, describing it as antithetical to his own Christian values.
"A year ago no one in Hill offices knew what effective altruism was," Leamer said. Build American AI is linked to Leading the Future, a political campaign group funded by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, a major midterms Republican donor.
Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which says it is focused on AI policy in the public interest, said that Trump allies are trying discredit anyone pushing for meaningful AI regulation, an idea that now has significant momentum.
"In D.C., at least, and maybe in the broader culture, we won that fight. The vibe is with us," said Carson, who also leads a political advocacy organization funded in part by Anthropic. "People are very concerned. Congress wants to regulate."
But leaders of AI evaluation start-ups that did not grow out of the AI safety movement said some Washington Republicans are distrustful of the label.
"It almost felt like a new version of McCarthyism," said Rayan Krishnan, CEO of the Andreessen Horowitz-backed start-up Vals AI, after a trip to Washington last month to pitch his start-up to the public sector.
Judd Rosenblatt, CEO of AE Studio, who described himself as a conservative small business owner, said multiple people in the Trump administration have told his team that they see the need for third parties to assess AI tools, but are wary of effective altruism, he said.
Civil society groups that have been auditing AI systems since before the debut of ChatGPT warn there is a risk that an opportunity for oversight of opaque AI giants will be squandered.
"Where we find ourselves now is trying to determine who will actually be in the room in making decisions," said Miranda Bogen, chief technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology and director of the advocacy group's AI Governance Lab, one of various groups eager to contribute their expertise in standard-setting.
The accord signed by AI chief executives last week, which Trump called "morally binding," was frequently mentioned onstage and in huddles between sessions at the Berkeley conference last weekend, where attendees endured a heat wave with fans and Popsicles.
At a Sunday discussion panel on what the AI auditor ecosystem might look like, one speaker said they are working on building a broad coalition of experts, including people working on bias and discrimination as well as blue-chip firms like Accenture and Deloitte. Panelists also discussed other ways the community could prove its legitimacy. Another suggested two-month boot camps to train a talent pipeline of qualified auditors.
Adam Gleave, CEO of FAR.AI, a nonprofit research institute, said in an interview that excluding the AI safety community would shut out people with expertise that are important in the current moment.
"When it comes to looking at millions of agent transcripts and trying to piece together what they did and how they were interacting, I don't think there are many organizations in the world that have that expertise," Gleave said. "The reality is that anyone you hire with that background is going to have some connection to the industry."
On his podcast, Sacks and his co-hosts, who remain close to the White House, made clear that they preferred instead to have established corporate giants do the work.
"You're going to see EY in short order here announce something," said investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who earlier in the episode said his start-up 8090 was building the global accounting firm formerly known as Ernst & Young "an entire audit infrastructure for super intelligence," and that 8090 now plans to "roll it out to everybody."
EY said in a statement that it was working with 8090 to "develop new capabilities that bring greater visibility, traceability and human accountability to consequential AI-enabled decisions and workflows."

articles.title_orig: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.title_zh: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.content_orig:
Rising rent puts an end to the dim sum and Sichuan restaurant that has been in the neighborhood for almost 15 years.
Mama Ji’s (opens in new tab) in the Castro was filled with diners Monday night. Waiters bustled around, moving between the compact dining room and sidewalk tables, shuttling plates of kung pao shrimp, triple “C” wings, and hot-and-numbing fish. They told diners about the night’s special, inspired by the most recent trip Lily Ji — customers know her as Mama Ji — took to the Sichuan province of China: crispy lotus-root cake topped with minced pork in fish sauce.
Judging by how busy the restaurant was, you’d never guess it would likely be diners’ final visits. The last day of service for Mama Ji’s, which opened almost 15 years ago, is set for Oct. 31.
Ji and her husband, Marv Wolpa, posted a letter on the door sharing the news and expressing gratitude for the neighbors who have supported their mom-and-pop restaurant but saying it is time for them to put their time and energy into their personal lives. “Work is a lot; I won’t miss the work,” Ji said. “But I will miss the people.”
In an interview with The Standard, Ji gave more context to the closure: The landlord had raised the rent, citing rising insurance costs and an inability to charge more for the residential unit above Mama Ji’s. “I said, ‘Whatever that’s your decision,’” Ji said. “That’s my decision to not continue.”
The couple, who are Castro residents, started serving the food Ji grew up eating as a pop-up, then transitioned to the full restaurant in 2013. Over the decade and a half the couple served their neighborhood, Mama Ji’s became a staple of the neighborhood.
One couple dining Monday night expressed their sadness. The waiter repeated what the letter said, noting that Ji and Wolpa are ready to retire. “All things in the world must end,” he concluded as he walked away.
As for Ji, she didn’t miss a beat when asked about what she plans to do next: “Relax!”
Madeline Taub is a food reporter intern at The Standard. She was previously a contributor to Cityside’s food publication, East Bay Nosh. She graduated from UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.
