articles.title_orig: Mark Mortimer, 'Another World' soap star, dies at 59
articles.title_zh: Mark Mortimer, 'Another World' soap star, dies at 59
articles.content_orig:
Mark Mortimer, best known for his role in the soap opera "Another World" in the '90s, died after "a fearless journey with cancer." He was 59 years old.
Mortimer died on Sept. 23, according to his obituary .
"He was an Army veteran, a model, an actor, an entrepreneur and a builder. He was a husband, father, son, brother and friend," his obituary said. "He was curious and determined, willing to take chances, start something new, change direction and figure things out along the way.
"But of all the titles Mark held throughout his life, the two that mattered most to him were husband and dad."
He acted in 81 episodes of "Another World" as Nick Hudson, appearing on the show from 1996 until the show's end in 1999, Variety and People reported.
He was first diagnosed with cancer in 2024. After that, he and his wife, Christie, founded the Integrative Access Foundation .
"Throughout Mark's journey, we met countless others who wanted more options but didn’t know where to turn, couldn’t afford the care, or were told their questions didn’t belong in traditional settings. The gap was clear, and it was deeply personal," according to the Integrative Access Foundation website. "Integrative Access was born from this experience."
Mortimer is survived by his wife, his daughter, Hunter, as well as his parents and several siblings.

articles.title_orig: Major champions, Hall of Famers fill 2026 World Champions Cup rosters
articles.title_zh: Major champions, Hall of Famers fill 2026 World Champions Cup rosters
articles.content_orig:
Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
European Team captain Darren Clarke, International Team captain Retief Goosen and United States Team captain Justin Leonard unveiled their rosters featuring major champions, World Golf Hall of Fame members and some of the most recognizable names in professional golf Monday for the 2026 Skechers World Champions Cup supporting Shriners Children’s.
The three teams will compete Dec. 3-6 at Feather Sound Country Club in Clearwater, Florida, in the event’s distinctive head-to-head format.
“Claiming the title last year was incredibly special, and I couldn’t be more excited to bring this European Team back together to defend in 2026,” Clarke said in a statement. “There’s a tremendous amount of pride that comes with representing Europe, and this group understands what it means to compete for one another. We know the U.S. and International Teams will be coming in strong, and we wouldn’t want it any other way as we look to top our winning score of 230 points. We’re looking forward to getting back to Feather Sound Country Club and doing everything we can to keep that trophy in European hands.”
The final two spots on each of the teams are play-in positions and will be determined based on the Charles Schwab Cup standings at the end of the regular season, which concludes at the SAS Championship, Oct. 16-18. These two spots will consist of a sixth player on each team as well as a playing vice captain, a new addition this year. The playing vice captain can be substituted in for one player in each round.
Bernhard Langer, pictured with his granddaughter Stella during the par 3 contest at the 2026 Masters, will play for the European Team.
Clarke returns to lead the European Team, joined by vice captain Jesper Parnevik, as well as Colin Montgomerie, Bernhard Langer, Miguel Angel Jimenez and newcomer Henrik Stenson.
The European roster includes major champions, Ryder Cup legends and some of the most successful players in the history of golf. Stenson, the 2016 Open champion who debuted on PGA Tour Champions this summer after leaving LIV Golf, will make his first appearance this year.
Clarke is back as captain for the third time. He led the Euros to a win in 2025. The Northern Irishman is the 2011 Open Championship winner, a six-time PGA Tour Champions winner and a five-time Ryder Cup team member who also captained the European Ryder Cup Team in 2016. In 2022, Clarke became the fourth player in history to win both the Open Championship and the Senior Open Championship.
Parnevik will return as vice captain for the Europeans. The native of Stockholm, Sweden, is a five- time PGA Tour winner and six-time international winner. Parnevik captured the 2016 Insperity Invitational on PGA Tour Champions and represented Team Europe in three Ryder Cups (1997, 1999, 2002). He competed in the World Champions Cup in 2023 and 2025, serving as a vice captain for the European Team in both competitions.
A member of the World Golf Hall of Fame, Montgomerie is widely regarded as one of the greatest Ryder Cup players of all time, having represented Europe eight times from 1991 to 2006 and having served as a captain for the winning European team in 2010.
Langer returns to play for the third time as the most accomplished player in PGA Tour Champions history with 47 victories and 12 senior major championships.
Jimenez brings with him an accomplished career spanning more than four decades. The Spaniard has recorded 17 PGA Tour Champions victories, 21 wins on the DP World Tour and three PGA Tour Champions majors.
Stenson makes his World Champions Cup debut. The Swede is a six-time PGA Tour winner, including victories at the Players Championship in 2009 and the Open Championship in 2016, becoming the first Swedish man to win a major championship.
Retief Goosen will lead the International Team.
Goosen, a two-time U.S. Open champion, will captain the Internationals, with Rod Pampling serving as vice captain alongside Vijay Singh, Scott Hend, Angel Cabrera and Steven Alker.
Pampling and Hend will each make their tournament debuts, joining an International team roster with extensive major championship, Presidents Cup and worldwide professional golf experience.
Goosen brings a Hall of Fame career to his role as captain. He won seven times on the PGA Tour and represented the International team in six Presidents Cups. He has five PGA Tour Champions wins, including the 2026 Mitsubishi Electric Classic. Goosen competed in the inaugural Skechers World Champions Cup in 2023.
Pampling, a native of Queensland, Australia, will make his debut as vice captain. He is a three-time PGA Tour winner and two-time PGA Tour Champions winner. He has also recorded multiple victories on the PGA Tour of Australasia.
Singh, a 2006 World Golf Hall of Fame inductee and three-time major champion, has won 34 times on the PGA Tour, including the 2000 Masters and the 1998 and 2004 PGA Championships. He spent 32 weeks as the world’s No. 1-ranked player.
Australia's Hend recorded 13 international victories, including 10 Asian Tour wins and a DP World Tour victory. He also won the Asian Tour Order of Merit in 2016 and has two Legends Tour victories.
Cabrera is a three-time PGA Tour winner, including major championship victories at the 2007 U.S. Open and 2009 Masters. The Argentina native has three PGA Tour Champions victories, including the Regions Tradition and Senior PGA Championship in 2025.
Alker is enjoying another standout season on PGA Tour Champions. The New Zealander has four wins in 2026, giving him 14 in his PGA Tour Champions career, and is a two-time Charles Schwab Cup champion. He's making his third appearance on the International Team.
Zach Johnson will play for the United States Team in the Skechers World Champions Cup Dec. 3-6 at the Feather Sound Country Club in Clearwater, Fla.
Justin Leonard will captain a formidable American roster alongside vice captain Billy Andrade and players Stewart Cink, Zach Johnson, Steve Stricker and Jerry Kelly.
Leonard is a two-time PGA Tour Champions winner and a 12-time PGA Tour winner whose career highlights include the 1997 Open Championship and the 1998 Players Championship. He made three Ryder Cup appearances for the U.S., including the memorable 1999 Ryder Cup at Brookline, where his 45-foot birdie putt on the 17th hole helped secure an American comeback. He represented the U.S. in five Presidents Cups and will represent the U.S. in the Skechers for the third time.
Andrade returns for the third time as U.S. vice captain. A four-time PGA Tour winner, Andrade later won three times on PGA Tour Champions in 2015, including the Charles Schwab Cup Championship, Boeing Classic and Bass Pro Shops Legends of Golf at Big Cedar Lodge. Andrade also represented the U.S. in the 1987 Walker Cup.
Cink brings an accomplished PGA Tour career and one of the strongest recent records on PGA Tour Champions. The eight-time PGA Tour winner has represented the U.S. in five Ryder Cups and four Presidents Cups. Since joining PGA Tour Champions, Cink has earned nine victories, including five wins so far this season. In 2025, he won the season-long race for the Charles Schwab Cup.
Johnson, a new addition to the U.S. Team, brings a 12-win PGA Tour career, two major championships and extensive international team experience to the U.S. side. The Iowa native won the 2007 Masters and 2015 Open and represented the U.S. in five Ryder Cups and four Presidents Cups.
Stricker returns for his third Skechers appearance. He has won 12 times on the PGA Tour and 18 times on PGA Tour Champions, including seven majors.
Kelly has earned 14 PGA Tour Champions victories, including three senior majors. He is a three-time PGA Tour winner and represented the U.S. in the 2003 Presidents Cup.
The Presidents Cup is nice and all, and extending what was already a lopsided winning streak is always fun. But the Presidents Cup isn’t the Ryder Cup.

articles.title_orig: Rubio calls for more information from Moscow after researcher’s suspected plague death
articles.title_zh: Rubio calls for more information from Moscow after researcher’s suspected plague death
articles.content_orig:
Health authorities in Siberia’s Irkutsk region have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation after a laboratory worker died from plague, according to media reports and a statement by a regional leader Friday.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, confirmed that the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague. Irkutsk officials had previously described the illness only as a “particularly dangerous infection.”
Citing information from Russia’s consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor and Buryatia’s government, Tsydenov said the woman had not visited his republic and that her infection was unrelated to the region.
“There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in areas bordering Mongolia,” he wrote on social media.
The woman was identified as Daria Sh., a 27- or 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk anti-plague institute, by the exiled news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) and pro-Kremlin broadcaster REN TV .
She reportedly told medical staff that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria while collecting samples for testing.
She was hospitalized Tuesday with symptoms of severe pneumonia in Shelekhov, a town near the regional capital of Irkutsk. She was placed on a ventilator and died Thursday, according to the reports.
The Shelekhov district hospital was placed under quarantine pending an assessment by a special commission.
At least 197 people who may have had contact with her were reportedly placed under medical isolation , including more than 100 in hospital wards.
Authorities canceled planned public events in Irkutsk, while law enforcement reportedly opened a criminal investigation into potential health safety violations resulting in death.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev urged the public to remain calm after meeting with Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova to coordinate emergency containment measures.
“All identified contact persons have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness, and their laboratory test results are negative,” Kobzev wrote on Telegram on Friday. He did not mention the reports of the laboratory worker’s death.
Media reports have described the suspected infection as pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs and can spread between humans through respiratory droplets. Tsydenov’s statement did not specify the form of plague.

We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help .
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $ 2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.

articles.title_orig: Google could soon solve Pixel's biggest face unlock flaw
articles.title_zh: Google could soon solve Pixel's biggest face unlock flaw
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Google’s modern face unlock on recent Pixel flagships is Class 3 biometric certified, but as anyone who has tried unlocking their phone in a dim bedroom knows, it is practically useless once the lights go down. That shortcoming has long fueled anticipation around Google’s secretive Project Toscana , an effort to overhaul facial authentication across Pixel devices, Chromebooks, and presumably Googlebooks by extension. Now, new code discovered in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 reveals that Google is actively building a “Face Active Illumination” system to help solve face unlock’s low-light authentication woes.
You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.
We’ve spotted several clues in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 suggesting Google is working on a “Face Active Illumination” feature for Pixel devices, at least, which could make face authentication more reliable in low-light conditions. The code points to dedicated toggles for activating the feature, controlling its brightness, and specifying when it should be allowed to activate, but it doesn’t reveal exactly which hardware provides the illumination.
While we managed to activate the feature, we could only get an incomplete and seemingly empty UI to appear at this stage. Strings within the app (other than the “Do Not Disturb” text) are also obfuscated, so there’s still a fair bit of mystery around this feature, how it would work, and what it could even be called for its final marketing name.
From the UI, we can infer that the “Face Active Illumination” feature is within the Face Unlock settings and may offer three brightness levels via a slider. When read with the code, the toggles could let users choose whether illumination will be used in dark environments (maybe referring to dark mode?), during bedtime hours, during Do Not Disturb, and while driving.
It’s unclear whether Face Active Illumination uses IR technology, as previously spotted under Project Toscana, or is merely ramping up screen brightness to throw more light on your face for easier face unlock. The presence of toggles doesn’t instill confidence for the former, as users wouldn’t need granular control over an IR-based system, much like we see (or quite literally, don’t see) with Face ID on the iPhone. It is thus likely to be the latter, as the toggles would allow users to avoid flashbanging themselves with their phone display in certain low-light situations.
Google hasn’t announced any details about Face Active Illumination or Project Toscana, and there’s a fair chance the two aren’t related. We’ll keep you updated when we learn more details about either.

articles.title_orig: CWC27 ticket applications surpass one million
articles.title_zh: CWC27 ticket applications surpass one million
articles.content_orig:
Ticket demand for the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup 2027 has surged past the one-million mark, with more than one million applications submitted in less than three days since the ticket ballot opened on 1 October 2026.
Over 320,000 fans have already registered for the ballot, submitting applications for matches across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia as anticipation continues to build for the 14th edition of the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup.
The India vs Pakistan fixture on 10 October is currently attracting the highest demand, with more than 100,000 ticket applications received. South Africa vs India follows with more than 86,000 applications, while India vs Australia has attracted more than 80,000.
The pre-seeded Super 7 fixture between India (A1) and Pakistan (A3) on 7 November has received almost 75,000 applications, making it the fourth most in-demand match. The 21 November Final has also proved popular , with almost 65,000 applications already submitted.
The tournament will feature 14 of the world’s best teams , with the first ball set to be bowled on 2 October and the Final scheduled for 21 November.
With excitement building across the three host nations, the ICC has opened the ticket ballot to give fans around the world the opportunity to register for a chance to attend the tournament.
Breaking down the new Cricket World Cup format | CWC27
A new format awaits at the 2027 Cricket World Cup!  
Crystal Arnold takes us through what to expect as South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia prepare to co-host the tournament.
Ticket prices range from USD $9.62 (R158) for entry-level tickets to USD $31.31 (R514) for the highest-tier matches. Special consideration has also been given to family bundles, student and pensioner pricing, early-bird local allocations, and community club and school group pricing.
ICC CEO, Sanjog Gupta said: “One million ticket applications in just over 48 hours of opening the ticket ballot is a demonstration of the attention, stature and affiliation for ICC Cricket World Cup 2027. ICC events are now spectacles which transcend cultural and geographic boundaries and serve as platforms to widen and deepen fandom for the sport.
“This is also Africa's moment to shine as an ICC marquee men's event is returning to the continent after two decades and brings with it the attention of 2.5 billion cricket fans across 120+ countries. We aim to ‘make the circle bigger’, for fans, for the athletes, for the game, and for communities who will gather to celebrate the competition and the culture. The ballot is open, and we can't wait to host the world so get in if you haven't already.”
Fans have until 23h59 (CAT) on 21 November to register for the ballot and select their desired matches at tickets.cricketworldcup.com .

articles.title_orig: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes | US midterm elections 2026
articles.title_zh: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes | US midterm elections 2026
articles.content_orig:
Polls show GOP candidates trailing Democrats in Senate races, and Republicans also struggling in House contests
Thirty days remain until the midterm elections, and Donald Trump and his Republican allies are pulling out all the stops to maintain control of Congress.
Super Pacs aligned with the GOP have already spent hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising and voter outreach in races expected to decide the majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, and plan to spend even more before the election is over. The president, Vice-President JD Vance, and other top Republicans are fanning out across the country to stump for vulnerable lawmakers.
So far, there are no signs the money or the rallies have improved what appears to be a grim state of affairs for Republicans , less than two years after their resounding victories in the 2024 election. Recently released polls continue to show the party’s candidates trailing their Democratic challengers in the Senate races that will decide the majority and control of the chamber.
“Candidate quality is beating gobs of Republican money,” the Senate’s Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, quipped over the weekend, when the New York Times released the latest in a series of closely watched polls that confirmed the momentum behind their bid to retake the Senate.
The surveys, conducted with Siena University, found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas – all states Trump won by double digits two years ago. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years , the party’s candidate Adam Hamilton was neck-and-neck with the Republican senator Roger Marshall, while in Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is narrowly trailing the Republican candidate, Ashley Hinson. Democratic candidates for governor were also leading in many traditionally Republican states, the Times and Siena found .
“If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races [would] go blue,” Briscoe Cain, a Republican state representative in Texas wrote on X Monday. The Democrats’ Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa were both leading in the Times and Siena survey.
“Republican voters feel too comfortable and are not as intense about this election as they should be. We have more voters than the left in Texas, but we have to vote,” Cain added.
Last Friday, the news outlet Semafor reported that the Senate Leadership Fund, a major GOP Super Pac, planned to pull money from the campaign of its candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, in favor of upping support for Marshall in Kansas. No Democrat has won a US Senate election in North Carolina since 2008, but Whatley has trailed in polls for months. Democrats need to win at least four seats in the chamber to regain the majority they lost in the 2024 election.
The situation for Democrats appears to be similarly positive in their campaign to retake the House, which Republicans control only narrowly. A CBS News and YouGov poll released on Sunday found Democrats with a nine percentage point lead on the generic ballot, an important indicator of voter intention in congressional races.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday found Trump’s approval ratings remained at the lowest point of his career, with only 32% of adult respondents approving of his performance as president. Independent voters – whose views often make the difference in close races – planned to back Democrats by a 16-percentage-point margin, though many remained undecided.
The president’s poor marks are believed to be a major cause of the Republican candidates’ struggles nationwide, but are far from the only one. Discontent over the state of the economy – particularly the price of gasoline and other consumer staples – is another reason, as is the on-again, off-again conflict with Iran, and concern over Trump’s hardline approach to enforcing immigration laws.
Republicans maintain they have avenues to victory in both chambers of Congress. Eight House Republicans represent districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, as opposed to 22 House Democrats representing districts Trump won – a number that has grown larger thanks to the unprecedented redistricting war Trump instigated. Many polls show voters have an unfavorable perception of the Democratic party, though views of Republicans are similarly negative. And despite strong fundraising by some Democratic candidates, Republicans and groups allied with their agenda have an edge in cash to spend on this election.
It may not be enough to halt the disintegration that appears to be occurring in the coalition that elected Trump two years ago. Only 26% of Hispanic voters – who swung towards Trump after years of leaning Democratic – plan to vote for Republicans this year, while 52% prefer the Democrats, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
“We’ve been seeing among Latino voters, as we’ve been seeing kind of in the electorate as a whole, a real strong rejection of the Trump administration, and that has inflated into an increase in support for Democratic candidates,” said Maria Isabel Di Franco Quinonez, a senior research director at Equis Research, a progressive firm that focuses on the community.
Should the trend hold, it could bode well for Democrats’ hopes in states and districts with large Latino populations. The effect may be pronounced in Texas, where the Republican leaders drew new congressional maps to favor their candidates, but only if Latino voters continue voting the way they did in 2024.
“If we see those levels continue to rise and see those districts look more like the kinds of support levels for Democrats that we had seen back in 2018, then that would result in maybe Republicans get one more seat after redrawing all the lines, as opposed to getting four or five more seats,” Quinonez said.

articles.title_orig: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.title_zh: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.content_orig:
By Jamie Durrani 2026-10-06T13:33:00+01:00
Source: © Nobel Prize Outreach/Niklas Elmehed
Francis Halzen is the first solo winner of the physics prize for more than 30 years
The 2026 Nobel prize in physics has been awarded to Belgian astrophysicist Francis Halzen for his work on the detection of high-energy cosmic neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy. Halzen spearheaded the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, which has enabled scientists to track high-energy neutrinos that have reached Earth from the farthest reaches of the universe. It is the first time that the physics prize has been awarded to an individual recipient since 1992, when Georges Charpak was recognised for his work on particle detectors .
Neutrinos are elementary particles released by many different sources, including radioactive substances, the sun and other celestial bodies. But the neutrinos released by highly energetic processes like giant supernovae in the distant universe can have energies far higher than other cosmic neutrinos. As a result, these high-energy neutrinos – which have no charge and almost no mass – travel across the universe barely interacting with other matter and without changing direction or losing energy. This means that when these neutrinos reach the Earth they carry information about extreme environments in distant regions of space that cannot be gathered by monitoring other types of radiation such as light or gamma rays.
But the very properties that make high-energy cosmic neutrinos such useful carriers of information also make them incredibly difficult to detect. In the 1980s, Halzen came up with the idea of building a giant facility at the South Pole, where flashes of blue light given off as neutrinos pass through the Antarctic ice could be tracked. Halzen and his colleague John Learned presented the concept at a conference in Poland in June 1988.
Source: © Johan Jamestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
The IceCube neutrino observatory is a huge cubic kilometre of ice dotted with sensors that was the brainchild of Halzen
Since then, Halzen, who works at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US, has spent years developing techniques to detect neutrinos, contributing to projects in Greenland and Antarctica that honed the technology. Eventually, he led an initiative that culminated in the construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, in which more than 5000 special sensors are spread across a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice deep below the surface.
The IceCube facility was completed in 2011, and uncovered the first evidence of high-energy cosmic neutrinos just two years later. The project involves more than 450 researchers from 14 countries and has paved the way for further international collaboration to detect cosmic neutrinos. Speaking at the prize announcement, the Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce noted that a global network of neutrino telescopes, based in ice and the oceans, is currently being established, which will allow researchers to ‘monitor all of the sky, all of the time’.
Speaking on the phone immediately after the announcement, Halzen described the award as ‘a great surprise’ and emphasised the critical contributions from his collaborators over the years. ‘When we started this project, everybody realised this was a good idea, but very few thought it would work – including myself,’ he said. ‘So this was an adventure where success was not guaranteed and we were lucky to overcome the various challenges, partly because the talent of collaborators and partly because of luck. It was a long journey, but it finally worked.’
Chemistry World will be bringing you all the news and analysis on the Nobel prize in chemistry in the run up to the announcement at 11.45 GMT (10.45 BST) tomorrow 7 October. Following the announcement we’ll be hosting a free webinar to explore the impact of this Nobel-prize winning research with an expert panel on Friday 9 October 16.00 GMT (15.00 BST) .
By Mariana Kneppers , Jamie Durrani and Neil Withers

articles.title_orig: EU Commission throws down the gauntlet on reforming the bloc
articles.title_zh: EU Commission throws down the gauntlet on reforming the bloc
articles.content_orig:
The European Commission has put forward far-reaching proposals, including cutting the number of commissioners and moving away from unanimity, testing member states' appetite for internal reforms that stop short of treaty change.
The proposals are part of a broader package to make the EU's structures and decision-making fit for a membership of 30 or more countries. They are bound to be controversial among European capitals.
"The main question has been: is the EU fit for another enlargement? And there is a clear yes, a future enlargement is possible. Our assessment shows that in most policy areas, the EU is already fit for enlargement," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters.
The Commission proposes identifying areas where so-called passerelle clauses could be activated, allowing the Council to move from unanimity to qualified majority. Activating those clauses, however, itself requires unanimity.
The idea of extending qualified majority voting is not new, particularly in foreign and security policy, where a veto can undermine the EU's ability to project geopolitical weight abroad.
Last month, 11 countries including France and Germany circulated a joint letter calling for the bloc to explore curbing obstructive foreign policy vetoes on the basis of sincere cooperation, notably through greater use of constructive abstention.
Asked whether member states back the move, Kos acknowledged that positions differ widely among EU countries. "It will not be easy, but it is worth trying," she said. A specific area she identified where less unanimity could be used is precisely during accession processes.
"Our proposal is to make our decision-making process more effective. We suggest using more QMV [qualified majority voting], which is nothing new. What is new is that we are suggesting that we will reduce the number of unanimity decisions in the accession process," Kos said.
Unanimity is required to grant a country candidate status and to close negotiations. In between, however, the current methodology gives any member state a veto over 150 steps.
The Commission also wants to make more use of enhanced cooperation, which lets at least nine member states pursue deeper integration on matters of crucial or strategic interest where blockages persist.
The most recent examples are the Ukraine Support Loan, from which Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out, and the European Public Prosecutor's Office.
Here too, Brussels may meet resistance from some capitals, notably the so-called "Friends of the Western Balkans", a group that includes Italy and Austria. They have pushed back against differentiated membership and regulatory asymmetry.
The Commission is also proposing to drop the principle that every EU country has a commissioner, which could prove problematic in a Union of 30 or more members.
Under the Lisbon Treaty, the Commission should have a number of members equal to two-thirds of the member states, chosen by "strictly equal rotation" that reflects the demographic and geographical range of all EU countries.
The system never took effect. In 2013, the European Council unanimously decided to keep one commissioner per member state, a concession to Ireland to secure a yes vote in its second referendum on the Lisbon Treaty.
Ireland was merely the most vocal opponent of losing a permanent presence in the Commission. Small member states widely fear their voice would be harder to hear in Brussels.
Rotation could also be hard to swallow for large countries such as France and Germany, which might find themselves left out of the College of Commissioners while the likes of Malta or Luxembourg are included.
"There are some candidates who say, no worries, this country can represent us. Other countries who say, yes, but not at the beginning. We would like to see how it [the Commission] works," Kos added.
The proposal for a leaner EU executive is well timed. The Commission is undergoing a so-called "large-scale review", and capitals are in intense talks on the bloc's next long-term budget, in which the EU administration is likely to face deep cuts.
Proposals that mainly affect candidate countries, such as safeguards against democratic backsliding and gradual integration, are likely to meet less resistance.
However, supporters of the reforms point out that, as candidates edge closer to joining the bloc, the question of how to keep an enlarged Union effective will be harder to dismiss.
Still, the suggestion is sure to raise eyebrows among European governments. Four EU diplomats who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity said these internal reforms are unlikely to fly.
The first test will come next week, when the enlargement reforms will land on the table of the EU leaders gathered for the European Council on 15-16 October.
"Some things are drafted to be killed," an EU diplomat said.

articles.title_orig: Meet the artist who built a giant spider for a virtual world
articles.title_zh: Meet the artist who built a giant spider for a virtual world
articles.content_orig:
Explore the “Feral Metaverse” of Theo Triantafyllidis, the winner of the 2026 Frieze London Artist Award, which is co-commissioned and co-produced with Forma in collaboration with Google Arts & Culture.
Vice President & Founder, Google Arts & Culture
Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder Athens
Your browser does not support the audio element.
Artist Theo Triantafyllidis won this year’s Frieze Artist Award for his interactive sculpture, "Feral Metaverse (Spider)." This climbable, giant spider structure invites visitors to cooperate in both physical and digital gaming environments. You can see this collaborative project at Frieze London from October 14–18 or visit Google Arts & Culture to explore how the team used artificial intelligence to build it.
Artist Theo Triantafyllidis built a giant, climbable spider sculpture that doubles as a multiplayer video game. He worked with a huge team and used AI to help design the game’s look and digital world. Visitors have to help each other climb the spider to play, which encourages people to work together. It’s a cool way to show how art and technology can bring people closer.
Athens-based artist Theo Triantafyllidis is the recipient of this year’s Frieze Artist Award, which supports artists at pivotal moments in their careers as they create ambitious new work. Triantafyllidis works with video games, live simulations, performances, and physical installations to build playful worlds exploring complex phenomena. At Frieze London, he’ll present 'Feral Metaverse (Spider), 2026,' a participatory climbable spider sculpture and live multiplayer game rooted in shared experiences.
In Triantafyllidis’ words, “spiders are the original engineers.” Strange, intelligent and unexpectedly tender, the spider became a central figure for an artwork built around physical contact, cooperation, and play.
Theo Triantafyllidis, Photo: Paris Tavitian, Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder, Athens.
From afar, the giant spider-shaped structure might appear intimidating, but up close, its softness invites touch. Visitors are encouraged to help one another climb the sculpture. Once players are aboard the legs, the experience extends into the Feral Metaverse, a shared digital environment where players collaborate, move, and form temporary collective bodies together.
Theo Triantafyllidis, 'Feral Metaverse (Spider), 2026.' Game still. Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder, Athens.
The award allowed Triantafyllidis to expand his team of sculptors, fabricators, textile designers, game developers, and civil engineers. For this project, the group introduced Gemini into their workflow, working with it as a tool and collaborator as they generated the sketches, character designs, backdrops, and 3D renders that shaped the look and feel of the game. In rendering AI outputs as sculptural material, they were able to push both the game and the audience interaction with it.
The experience, which requires players to watch each other, exchange advice, and learn together, will move between the screen and the booth at Frieze. It’s a testament to how both public and online spaces can foster cooperation and warmth.
Visit Google Arts & Culture to learn more about the making of the work, which will be on display at Frieze London in The Regent’s Park from October 14–18.

articles.title_orig: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come
articles.title_zh: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come
articles.content_orig:
CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.
Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive.
"I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.
Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential , questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next.
Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list .
Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity.
For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."
For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology.
"You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."
Ibrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.
Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:
That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said.
With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce .
"They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."
Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens."
"One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.
Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.title_orig: N.C. A&T Alumnus Featured in Netflix Reboot of “A Different World” - North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University
articles.title_zh: N.C. A&T Alumnus Featured in Netflix Reboot of “A Different World” - North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University
articles.source: North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University
articles.content_orig:
By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

articles.title_orig: One year to go: Cape Town begins countdown to 2027 World Mountain and Trail Running Championships
articles.title_zh: One year to go: Cape Town begins countdown to 2027 World Mountain and Trail Running Championships
articles.content_orig:
South African trail runner Toni McCann ( © WMTRC Cape Town 2027 Zac Zinn )
From 6 to 10 October 2027, Cape Town will welcome the world's best mountain and trail runners for the 2027 World Mountain and Trail Running Championships (WMTRC), a landmark event that will place Africa at the centre of the global off-road running community.
“Mountain and trail running is experiencing a real boom, and the fourth staging of the World Mountain and Trail Running Championships is another cause for celebration,” said World Athletics President Sebastian Coe. “As the first World Mountain and Trail Running Championships to be hosted in Africa, this is an important milestone for our sport and one for which excitement continues to build now the event is only one year away. We look forward to another successful edition of this global championships, one that brings together the world’s best elite athletes and mass participation runners for a festival of off-road running.”
Sarah Rowell, Nadeem Khan and Janet Ng, respective presidents of the World Mountain Running Association, the International Association of Ultrarunners and the International Trail Running Association, said: “With one year to go until the fourth World Mountain and Trail Running Championships, it is clear that the excitement around the event continues to grow. Member Federations are planning their trials and athletes and their coaches their training for what will be stunning and competitive races set against the backdrop of Table Mountain. As event partners, we have been impressed by the professionalism of the local organising committee and we continue to work closely with them to deliver a successful event in October 2027.”
WMTRC Cape Town 2027 will be the first World Mountain and Trail Running Championships ever hosted in Africa and the first World Championship in an athletics discipline staged in South Africa since 1993. Hosted by Golazo South Africa, Athletics South Africa and Western Province Athletics, the championship represents a defining moment for South African athletics, African sport and the continued growth of mountain and trail running worldwide.
Individual and team world titles will be contested across all disciplines, bringing together the world's elite mountain and trail runners. The championship programme will feature the sport's premier disciplines:
• Uphill • Classic • Classic U20 • Short Trail • Long Trail
A programme of mass participation events is also being developed, allowing more than 2000 amateur runners from South Africa and around the world to experience the championship atmosphere and compete on selected championship terrain. It will make the championships even more memorable and provide many sports enthusiasts with a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Further details on these events will be announced in due course.
"With one year to go, Athletics South Africa is proud to be part of a historic moment as we prepare to welcome the world to the first World Mountain and Trail Running Championships ever hosted in Africa,” said Athletics South Africa Acting CEO Terrence Magogodela. “Cape Town 2027 provides an extraordinary opportunity to showcase South Africa's athletes, landscapes and hospitality, while creating a lasting legacy for mountain and trail running across our country and continent. Through our national championship and selection pathway, we are committed to ensuring that Team South Africa is ready to compete with the world's best when the championships arrive next October.”
Beyond the world titles, WMTRC Cape Town 2027 aims to leave a lasting legacy through athlete development, greater participation and international exposure. Bringing the championship to Africa creates an opportunity to grow the sport across the continent and introduce more runners to its exceptional mountain and trail destinations.
“I am so proud that Cape Town will host Africa's first World Mountain and Trail Running Championships,” said South African international trail runner Toni McCann. “It's incredibly exciting to welcome the world's best athletes to experience the energy of this city: its people, our passionate trail and running community, the diversity of our natural spaces and the magical beauty of our rugged trails. Beyond that, this event has the power to make a lasting impact on a new generation of South African runners who dream of one day wearing the green and gold.”
As the countdown enters its final year, WMTRC Cape Town 2027 is poised to become more than a championship. It is an opportunity to showcase Africa to the world, elevate mountain and trail running across the continent and create a lasting legacy for future generations of athletes.
One world stage. A new continent. Mountain and trail running's next chapter.

articles.title_orig: World Food Programme convoy attacked in Sudan
articles.title_zh: World Food Programme convoy attacked in Sudan
articles.content_orig:
By Davide Dionisi and Kielce Gussie
On the evening of October 5, the United Nations spokesperson Farhan Haq announced the latest tragedy in Sudan while speaking to journalists: âAn airstrike in South Kordofan targeting two trucks belonging to the World Food Programme (WFP) killed a driver and damaged food supplies. In a second incident, a child was killed and twelve others were injured: five boys and seven girls.â
In a statement , the WFP stressed that the two trucks were clearly marked and the attack comes just one day after another WFP truck hit an explosive device after delivering food aid in Dilling.
Furthermore, the statement explained how these attacks show âthe increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need.â Despite the risks, the UN organization stressed its commitment to providing support and aid to those in need.
In 2025, the UN aid coordination office OCHA reported more than 30 million people are in need of humantiarian assistance.
The Sudanese army has been fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, following disagreements between the two sides over issues such as the integration of their respective forces as part of the transition towards civilian government. Last month, the US State Department said that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the RSF, nor their respective leaders, ârepresent a legitimate and constitutional government for Sudan.â
The conflict has forced more than 14 million people to flee their homes and has triggered waves of ethnically motivated killings. According to the United Nations, more than seven million people, particularly in Darfur, are living in conditions of food insecurity.
After months of deadlock, the US is seeking to revive diplomatic efforts to find a solution to the conflict.
âWe reaffirm the United Statesâ steadfast commitment, together with our Egyptian partners and other regional and international allies, to promoting a political solution to the crisis,â said Massad Boulos, the US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs, in a post on X. He said he had attended a luncheon hosted by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of the Sudanese army.
The Egyptian president stressed that âEgypt will continue to make every possible effort, at the regional and international levels, to promote a political solution to the crisis, help bring the war to an end, and alleviate the humanitarian suffering of the Sudanese people.â He added that this âwill enable Sudan to restore security and stability and embark on reconstruction.â
President Al-Sisi also reaffirmed to General Burhan his countryâs âunwavering supportâ for the âbrotherly Sudanese peopleâ and its commitment to preserving Sudanâs unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national institutions, including the regular army.
The meeting in Egypt came less than two weeks after Washington denied the Sudanese army chief a visa to attend a planned address to the United Nations General Assembly. According to Sudanese sources, the move was reportedly linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal, which Khartoum has so far resisted.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the U.S.
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the U.S.
articles.content_orig:
The state has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, health officials said Monday, making it the largest outbreak in the U.S. in more than three decades.
NEW YORK (AP) — Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 reported cases, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The nation has seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the past two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Since the beginning of last year, large outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest with 997 cases reported.
The governor of New York on Monday declared a disaster emergency because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extends the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and allows nurses to join doctors in ordering testing. The state has more than 100 cases this year.
Health officials say Pennsylvania’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia. There have been 1,004 cases, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths , state officials said.
Health experts attribute such outbreaks to low vaccination rates.
It’s been decades since a U.S. state has seen an outbreak surpass 1,000 cases, stretching back to a multiyear outbreak in New York City in the early 1990s that infected more than 4,500 people.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status .
Measles is highly contagious. It spreads when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, and through contaminated surfaces. It can also linger in the air for two hours. Up to 9 out of 10 people who are susceptible will get the virus if exposed, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
U.S. measles infections have been surging in recent years, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation.
Pennsylvania and New York are not the only states with a growing problem. Another is Ohio, with more than 200 cases this year. Like in Pennsylvania, some of the hardest-hit Ohio counties have significant Amish populations, which tend to have lower vaccination rates.
Meanwhile, CDC officials have quietly begun to acknowledge measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
State officials in August announced that two unvaccinated residents died after being infected with measles.
The announcement quickly came under fire as a clash erupted between vaccine-promoting Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines.
Since then, Pennsylvania has reported three additional deaths.
But for weeks, the CDC — which Kennedy oversees — did not count any deaths on its measles data dashboard, instead saying it was seeking more information. That changed two weeks ago, when one death was finally counted, and again last week when a second was added to the agency’s tally.

articles.title_orig: Flydubai pilot planned a 9/11-style attack on Tel Aviv airport, source says
articles.title_zh: Flydubai pilot planned a 9/11-style attack on Tel Aviv airport, source says
articles.content_orig:
TEL AVIV — The pilot who allegedly tried to bring down an Israel-bound flight had been planning a 9/11-style attack by crashing into the country’s main airport in Tel Aviv, a Middle Eastern official has told NBC News.
The pilot, identified by NBC News as Hamman al-Hamammi , told investigators Monday that he wanted to evade Israel’s defenses and crash into the Ben Gurion Airport or another building, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the person was not authorized to speak publicly.
An Omani citizen, multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East identified al-Hammami. Authorities have not officially released the identity.
He is currently being questioned by investigators in the United Arab Emirates after he was transferred from Saudi Arabia. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely, after last week’s dramatic midair incident.
Emirati authorities said Saturday that the pilot attacked his fellow pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar , with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls.
The jet which was carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers then plummeted 14,000 feet in just 29 seconds, according to data from the aviation tracking service Flightradar24, causing panic onboard.
Machchhar, an Indian national and a veteran pilot of 17 years, said in a call Friday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that his fellow pilot told him he was going to pray, something he didn’t consider unusual as observant Muslims pray five times a day.
A few minutes later, he said he felt a strong blow to the head. “Because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing, and I was completely blurred out,” he added. “The next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down.”
A video of the call was released by Netanyahu’s office.
Initially, Machchhar said, he thought there was “catastrophic damage to the aircraft,” but once the blows kept coming he “realized that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”
In a separate call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, also Friday, Machchhar said he managed to open the cockpit’s door on the second attempt, despite the blows raining down.
“I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door. And thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back,” he said.
Focus has shifted onto the missed security signals ahead of the flight.
Citing sources familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that al-Hammami had “previously been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.”
It is unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country with no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly the plane carrying Israelis to Tel Aviv.
According to Israeli law, airlines must provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, up to 48 hours before a flight.
Israeli investigators are leaning towards the assessment that the pilot was acting as a lone wolf, according to an Israeli official and a source familiar with the matter, although they said there is still more to learn about what led to his radicalization.
In the meantime, Netanyahu has called on the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects” of Israel’s civil aviation in the aftermath of the incident.
Elsewhere, Vice President JD Vance underlined the concerns potential security failures.
“That person should not have been flying an airline, and so we’re certainly looking at our procedures within the United States to make sure that people who are obviously flight risks are not getting behind the wheel of an airplane,” he told a reporter at Joint Base Andrews on Monday.
Keir Simmons is chief international correspondent for NBC News, based in Dubai.

articles.title_orig: Ranked: The World’s Richest Countries (2006-2026)
articles.title_zh: Ranked: The World’s Richest Countries (2006-2026)
articles.content_orig:
Measured by economic output per person, the world’s richest countries tend to be small, developed states found mostly in Europe. One South American country, though, has followed the Gulf state approach to greater riches.
This visualization ranks the countries with the highest GDP per capita in 2006, 2016, and 2026 using projections from the International Monetary Fund’s World Economic Outlook . Figures are in current prices and have been adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP).
In 2006, Liechtenstein already stood atop global rankings, with the only GDP per capita ($112,499) to reach six figures. The small Alpine microstate was followed by nearby Luxembourg ($96,014) as well as Gulf petrostates like Qatar ($86,252) and the United Arab Emirates ($74,230).
Most of the world’s wealthiest countries by this measurement are small offshore financial hubs such as Singapore and Switzerland.
The table below ranks the world’s top 20 countries by PPP-adjusted GDP per capita in 2006.
Different countries saw their economic fortunes grow through different means. Singapore, for example, developed internationally competitive industries, including semiconductors and pharmaceuticals . Off the strength of these industries the country eventually rose to have the second-highest GDP per capita ($173,708) worldwide in 2026.
Guyana’s transformation, by contrast, began with a resource discovery that changed the country’s economic profile altogether.
Oil production in Guyana only began in December 2019. As offshore output expanded, the impact extended beyond petroleum. Oil revenues have helped finance infrastructure and human capital programs, while public investment has supported construction and other domestic activity.
For a small economy, developing a major export industry can rapidly change output per resident. The country’s GDP per capita has grown more than anywhere else since 1990. By 2026, Guyana was projected to have a higher GDP per capita ($95,477) than any other country in the Western Hemisphere, including the United States ($94,430).
The challenge for Guyana is turning that windfall into lasting gains. Guyana has accumulated oil revenue in a Natural Resource Fund, helping balance current development needs with future savings. Investing effectively matters because oil prices can fluctuate sharply, and a higher national average does not automatically translate into better services or higher incomes for every household.
Ireland’s climb reflects a different kind of international connection: the role of multinational companies. Profits generated by foreign-owned multinationals contribute to domestic production even when they ultimately flow to owners abroad. This can create a substantial gap between the size of the economy and the income retained by residents.
Corporate restructuring can also produce unusually large jumps. In 2015, the relocation of company balance sheets to Ireland, including intellectual property, drove a dramatic increase in reported GDP. The Irish government has even set up a parallel measurement of economic output to account for these multinational firms’ activities.
By 2026 Ireland’s GDP per capita ($159,129) is forecast to be the second-highest in Europe and third-highest worldwide.

ASML is Europe’s most valuable listed company at $670 billion, but banks lead in 15 of the 42 countries covered.
Europe’s most valuable listed company makes the machines behind advanced chips. But across the continent, banks are far more likely to be a country’s stock-market leader.
This graphic shows the largest publicly traded company in 42 European countries based on company headquarter location and ranking them by market capitalization. It uses data from StockAnalysis.com and local stock-exchanges as of September 29, 2026, or the latest available quote.
ASML’s lead as Europe’s largest company reflects its unusual position in the booming chip supply chain. It is also the only technology company among the 42 national leaders.
At $670 billion, the Dutch company is worth almost twice as much as HSBC ($342.4 billion) or Roche ($341.5 billion), the largest companies in the UK and Switzerland.
The table below lists each European country’s most valuable listed company, along with its sector and market capitalization:
Figures rounded. Albania, Andorra, San Marino, and Vatican City have no publicly traded stocks.
As the only supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography systems, which chipmakers use to manufacture advanced processors, ASML ranks as the world’s 20th largest company by market cap .
Novo Nordisk, Denmark’s largest company at $168.6 billion, was once Europe’s most valuable at more than $650 billion in 2024. The maker of Ozempic and Wegovy has since lost more than 70% of that value as Eli Lilly’s rival GLP-1 drugs, Mounjaro and Zepbound, took market share.
Beyond ASML, finance and energy companies lead across Europe. Banks lead 15 countries, and including insurers and investment firms, finance leads 18. Energy and utilities companies lead another 10, so the two sectors account for 28 of the 42 national leaders.
Europe’s top companies are full of banks because of how its economy is built, with euro area firms having traditionally relied far more on bank loans than U.S. companies, which turn to capital markets.
Banks lead large markets as well as small ones, with Santander topping Spain at $205 billion and UniCredit leading Italy at $143 billion. In smaller markets, the leader is often a subsidiary of a Western European group: UniCredit controls Croatia’s Zagrebačka banka and the Bosnian bank on this list, and Germany’s Allianz owns Slovakia’s Slovenská poisťovňa.
Many energy leaders are state-controlled: the Norwegian state owns 67% of Equinor , and the Czech state holds nearly 70% of ČEZ .
Few newer companies have challenged these top-ranking European incumbents. A 2024 report by former ECB president Mario Draghi found that no EU company worth over €100 billion has been built from scratch in the last 50 years, while all six U.S. companies worth over €1 trillion were built in that time.
If you enjoyed today’s post, check out America’s Top 10 Biggest Semiconductor Firms on Voronoi.
Nearly 100 million car, buses, and trucks were built in 2025. Over a third of these came from just one country.
Factories around the world built nearly 100 million vehicles in 2025, led by major manufacturing hubs across Asia, North America, and Europe.
This graphic ranks 20 leading countries by reported vehicle production in 2025 using the latest figures from the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers (OICA). Figures generally cover both passenger and commercial vehicles, subject to country coverage specifications.
China set a new vehicle-production record in 2025, extending its 17-year run as the world’s largest producer. The country manufactured 34.5 million vehicles, more than triple U.S. production.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.title_zh: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President Vladimir Putin 's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump , meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.
Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution explicitly prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and the establishment of foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT .
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

articles.title_orig: Pumpkin named Bagheera breaks world record for Lymington grower
articles.title_zh: Pumpkin named Bagheera breaks world record for Lymington grower
articles.content_orig:
A pumpkin grower has set a new world record after producing a giant squash.
Ian Paton, from Lymington, Hampshire, entered his exceptionally large specimen into a giant vegetable weigh-off near Reading in Berkshire.
It weighed 2,856.8lbs (1,295.8kg), has circumference of over 20ft (6m) and was officially confirmed by Guinness World Records judge, Sebastian Suski.
Paton said growing the pumpkin named Bagheera, tending to it for up to six hours and providing about 130 gallons of water daily, had been "bloody hard work". It was the first time the 65-year-old, who has grown giant pumpkins with his twin brother Stuart for over 50 years, had entered the competition on his own.
The pumpkin is now on show at Sunnyfields farm near Southampton, where it will be displayed for the next few weeks.
The farm has used more than 10,000 pumpkins and squashes to create a giant pumpkin mural of Sir David Attenborough .
Paton said the pumpkin would later be used as feed for cows.

articles.title_orig: Growing potential for Invest 92L to intensify into Hurricane Isaias as data reveals its track uncertainty
articles.title_zh: Growing potential for Invest 92L to intensify into Hurricane Isaias as data reveals its track uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
Invest 92L is expected to strengthen into at least Tropical Storm Isaias in the Gulf this week. FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist Bryan Norcross breaks down all the possible scenarios and identifies which parts of the Gulf Coast could see the biggest impacts from this system.
A tropical depression is likely to form in the southern Gulf this week amid the quietest start to an Atlantic hurricane season since 1966, the start of the satellite era, with no hurricanes having formed this year.
THE LATEST FROM FOX WEATHER HURRICANE SPECIALIST BRYAN NORCROSS
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has designated a brewing tropical disturbance as Invest 92L, and is giving the system high odds of becoming at least a tropical depression over the next two days. From there, how strong this storm becomes and exactly where it tracks still remains an open question.
WHAT IS AN INVEST DURING HURRICANE SEASON?
The term "invest" is used every hurricane season in the Atlantic and the Eastern and Central Pacific basins, accompanied by a number from 90 to 99 and either the suffix "L," "E" or "C," respectively.
Currently, a massive cold front is draped over Central Florida and is extending across the Gulf, bringing days of heavy rain to the Sunshine State through the workweek.
A storm could develop at the tail end of this front sometime on Thursday or Friday, potentially developing a more defined center that forecasters can track.
CALIFORNIA DECLARES STATE OF EMERGENCY AS POTENTIALLY HISTORIC SUPER EL NIÑO LOOMS
However, Wednesday will be a crucial day in determining this system's future as it begins to interact with more hostile El Niño-driven winds as well as dry air, which have helped suppress the hurricane season in the Atlantic overall.
"A more defined system in the southern Gulf will be able to defend itself from the hostile conditions," the FOX Forecast Center said.
"Some models now are hinting at possibly our first hurricane of the season, but there is still a lot to fine tune as uncertainty remains extremely high."
CENTURIES-OLD LAVA ROCK ARCH IN HAWAI'I VOLCANOES NATIONAL PARK COLLAPSES INTO OCEAN FOLLOWING HURRICANE NOLO
The FOX Forecast Center said the system could also struggle to develop or remain closer to the coast of Mexico .
Regardless of tropical development, forecasts show another round of heavy rain headed to parts of the Florida and Louisiana coasts by the weekend.
NOAA's Weather Prediction Center (WPC) has issued a Level 2 out of 4 flash flood risk for parts of the Southeast on Friday and Saturday.
Meanwhile, Gulf water temperatures are currently at their warmest levels on record dating back to 1982. Warm waters are conducive for tropical development.
September ended without a hurricane for the first time in 32 years, despite it being the climatological peak of the season.
SEPTEMBER ENDS HURRICANE-FREE IN THE ATLANTIC FOR THE FIRST TIME IN 32 YEARS AMID IMPENDING SUPER EL NIÑO
A neighborhood destroyed in the aftermath of Hurricane Ian in Fort Myers, Florida.
(RICARDO ARDUENGO/AFP / Getty Images)
If the entire 2026 Atlantic hurricane season ends without a hurricane, it would mark the first hurricane-free Atlantic season of the modern era.

articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Google has a settings page problem across most of its apps: there are simply too many options in each one. That results in a settings page that is far more convoluted than users would like. Fortunately, the company seems to be taking note. Last month, we spotted Google working on a redesigned settings page in Gemini , and now it seems the company is trying to fix the Google app’s settings page as well.
You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.
While digging through the latest version of the Google app (v17.64.13), we found evidence of a redesign of the settings page in the works. Currently, the Google app’s settings page has a simple, straightforward layout. However, with the upcoming redesign, Google could switch to a card-based layout, grouping similar settings into cards and using labels to organize each card into categories such as “Your App Experience,” “Privacy & Safety,” and more.
The redesigned settings page aligns more closely with Google’s Material 3 Expressive design language. It could also bring some previously buried settings to the main settings screen. Settings for “Search personalization,” “SafeSearch,” and “Results about you” are displayed front and center on the upcoming settings page. Right now, these settings are buried inside the “Privacy & Safety” section.
This redesigned settings page still differs from the one we saw Google working on for the Gemini app. It is unclear whether this is intentional or simply Google’s inability to decide on a unified design style for its apps.
This new settings page UI hasn’t rolled out yet, and there is no way to tell when it will. We will keep an eye out for further changes and update you when we learn more.
